The enrolled population was both too advanced and too heterogeneous for a liver-directed treatment: 63 percent had macrovascular invasion, 16 percent were Child-Pugh B7 and the median tumour burden was 18 percent of the liver, and a post hoc subset with burden of 25 percent or less and ALBI grade 1 reached 21.9 against 17.0 months in favour of radioembolisation

The operational penalty fell entirely on one arm: a median 29 days from randomisation to radioembolisation against 7 days to sorafenib in a population whose median survival was about 9 months, so roughly a tenth of the available survival time was consumed by work-up in the experimental arm alone

Eligibility included three quite different clinical situations, advanced disease, recurrence after cure and failure of two rounds of chemoembolisation, with no stratification that would let the result be read for any one of them
The comparator is now historical, so the trial cannot say how radioembolisation performs against the immunotherapy doublets that have replaced sorafenib in first-line advanced disease

Quality of life and tolerability favoured radioembolisation, which in an open-label trial with a single procedure against a continuously dosed oral drug reflects the shape of the two treatments as much as their toxicity
The abstract gives serious adverse events in the sorafenib arm as 82 percent and the Results text as 81 percent, so the paper's own safety denominator is inconsistent
The sponsor manufactures the device tested and also funded the editorial assistance, and the paper reports no independent statistical analysis
29107679.n: 459 patients with BCLC C HCC, unresectable recurrence after previously cured HCC, or HCC after two failed rounds of chemoembolisation, randomised 1:1 at 25 French liver centres between December 2011 and March 2015 to Y-90 resin radioembolisation (237) or sorafenib (222); 63 percent had macrovascular invasion, 16 percent were Child-Pugh B7 and 22 percent of the radioembolisation arm never received the treatment
29107679.bottom_line: SARAH found no survival advantage for radioembolisation over sorafenib in locally advanced HCC (median 8.0 against 9.9 months, HR 1.15), with better tolerability and quality of life after radioembolisation. The negative result is substantially a delivery and dosing failure: 22 percent of the radioembolisation arm never received it, the per-protocol medians were identical, activity was prescribed by body surface area, and the trial's own later dose-response analysis showed survival of 14.1 against 6.1 months above and below a tumour absorbed dose of 100 Gy.
29107679.funding: Funded by Sirtex Medical, which makes the resin microspheres tested, and which also paid for editorial assistance

limitations: A high proportion of patients assigned radioembolisation never received it, which the authors list first
The EQ-5D instrument used for quality of life is not liver-specific
The BCLC C survival finding rests on a small sample and was not corrected for multiplicity, so the authors state it should be considered exploratory

The authors note that patients from five of the eleven participating countries had to travel to Singapore for work-up and treatment and then return home for follow-up, which caused progression, death and consent withdrawal before treatment
critique: The primary comparison is partly a test of logistics rather than of biology: 52 of 182 patients assigned radioembolisation never received it, 29 of them because they were found ineligible after randomisation, and all remained in the intention-to-treat analysis, while the median interval from randomisation to treatment was 21 days for radioembolisation against 3 days for sorafenib in a population surviving about 9 months

Every positive result, including progression-free survival, time to progression, 6-month survival and the BCLC C subgroup, appears only in the treated population, which is a post-randomisation selected group from which the patients too ill or too anatomically unsuitable to be treated have been removed

The protocol permitted only a single radioembolisation while the contemporaneous SARAH trial allowed repeat treatment and delivered more than one to 37 percent of treated patients, and activity was prescribed by body surface area or the partition model rather than by personalised dosimetry, so the trial may have tested an underdosed version of the therapy
Cross-border delivery of the intervention was built into the design, so the treatment arm carried an operational burden that no routine practice would impose and that the control arm did not share

The control arm, sorafenib monotherapy, has since been displaced by immunotherapy combinations, so an equivalence result against sorafenib does not position radioembolisation against current first-line care

The trial is described as a two-tailed superiority-or-detriment design, so a null result cannot be read as equivalence, yet the conclusion that overall survival did not differ is routinely cited as though it established that

Randomisation was stratified by centre and portal vein thrombosis only, in a trial spanning 11 countries with markedly different work-up pathways, and no stratification or adjustment for country or for travel requirement was applied

The published text carries numerous transcription errors in the figures and tables, including transposed medians in the survival panels, a garbled 6-month survival sentence with the control arm's confidence interval pasted into the treatment arm's slot, and minus signs rendered as digits, so the printed effect estimates cannot be taken at face value

Despite being described as investigator-initiated, the device manufacturer funded most of the investigators' research, the lead author sits on its speakers bureau and advisory board, and the manuscript was edited by a Sirtex-supported agency
29498924.n: 360 patients with BCLC B or C HCC confined to the liver, not amenable to curative treatment, randomised 1:1 at 27 centres in 11 Asia-Pacific countries between July 2010 and May 2016 to a single Y-90 resin radioembolisation (182) or sorafenib (178); 90 percent were Child-Pugh A and about 30 percent had portal vein thrombosis, and only 130 of 182 assigned radioembolisation received it
29498924.bottom_line: SIRveNIB found no survival difference between a single radioembolisation and sorafenib in locally advanced HCC (median 8.8 against 10.0 months by intention to treat), with fewer adverse events and a higher tumour response rate after radioembolisation. Its interpretation is dominated by delivery failure: 28.6 percent of patients assigned radioembolisation never received it against 9.0 percent assigned sorafenib, and every signal favouring radioembolisation appears only in the treated population.
29498924.funding: Investigator-initiated but extensively supported by Sirtex Medical, which makes the resin microspheres tested: the lead author declares honoraria, consultancy, speakers bureau membership and institutional research funding from Sirtex, most co-authors declare Sirtex research funding, and the manuscript's language editing was Sirtex-supported

limitations: All microwave ablations used a single device (Acculis Sulis VpMTA) when many commercially available systems differ in antenna design, frequency, probe number and power, so the result does not generalise across devices
Patients were excluded after randomisation for not receiving the allocated intervention or for immediate loss to follow-up, which forced a per-protocol rather than intention-to-treat analysis
Allocation used sealed opaque envelopes, which the authors call a non-optimal method of concealment and masking, and operators were not masked

The design assumed 2.7 percent local progression with microwave and 15.4 percent with radiofrequency ablation, which the authors concede was optimistic; the observed difference was much smaller than estimated
Only 11 lesions measured 3 to 4 cm, so the larger-lesion analysis in which microwave ablation might differ was not possible
Two years is short follow-up for BCLC 0 to A disease, and management after local tumour progression was not assessed in this report
The authors state that equivalence of the two techniques cannot be confirmed from a trial designed to assess superiority
critique: Randomisation was by patient but the primary endpoint was analysed lesion by lesion, with 38 percent of patients contributing two or three lesions; no clustering or random-effect adjustment is described, so the chi-square test on 98 versus 104 lesions treats correlated lesions as independent and overstates precision

The trial had almost no power for the difference actually seen: 78 lesions per arm were sized for a 12.7 percentage-point absolute gap, while the observed gap was 6 percentage points, so the p value of 0.27 is uninformative rather than reassuring, yet the Interpretation is written as a positive statement that progression was low with both methods

Lesions with residual unablated tumour at one month were re-treated and the authors state that follow-up began only once the lesion was deemed completely ablated, so the nine lesions most likely to progress had their clock reset and were removed from the primary endpoint window by design

The Methods justify using a raw proportion rather than a Kaplan-Meier estimate on the grounds that all lesions were assessable at 2 years, but the at-risk table under the progression figure shows only 44 radiofrequency and 52 microwave lesions at risk at 2 years with 48 and 41 censored, so the stated assumption is contradicted by the published figure

The captions of Figures 2 and 3 are transposed in the published article and two different log-rank p values appear for the same pair of curves (0.1854 and 0.8012), so the survival and local-progression analyses cannot be reconciled from the paper as printed

Ablation-zone volumes are given as 5.4 mm3 (SD 20.8) for microwave versus 28.4 mm3 (SD 21) for radiofrequency, p = 0.35, alongside lesion volumes of 4.3 and 5.4 mm3 in Table 2; these are physically impossible magnitudes with standard deviations several times the mean, and the conclusion that microwave ablation produces no larger necrosis zone rests on them

Baseline distribution of lesions differed between arms in ways that bear on ablation difficulty and heat-sink: segment II held 18 microwave versus 5 radiofrequency lesions, the right lobe 54 versus 66, and Child-Pugh B patients were 20 versus 27 percent; no adjustment or sensitivity analysis is reported

New distant intrahepatic foci appeared in 72 and 70 percent of lesions by 2 years and 13 to 16 percent of patients were transplanted and censored, so the primary endpoint was measured against a background in which nearly every patient developed new disease, and local progression cannot separate technique quality from tumour biology

ClinicalTrials.gov registration NCT02859753 postdates the close of enrolment in February 2015; the authors record only university-level registration in 2011, so the primary endpoint and the per-protocol analysis population cannot be checked against a pre-enrolment record

The five operators had 8 to 20 years of interventional oncology experience, but radiofrequency ablation was the established technique and microwave the newer one during 2011 to 2015; an operator learning curve favouring the control arm is neither measured nor discussed

The reported risk ratio of 1.62 is oriented with radiofrequency ablation as the numerator while the point estimate favours microwave ablation, and the paper never states the direction, so the only effect estimate in the abstract reads as if it disfavoured the experimental arm

The trial was funded by Microsulis (AngioDynamics), maker of the microwave device, the sponsor reviewed the manuscript, and the editing support was paid for from the same grant, yet the declaration of interests reads in full that the authors have no competing interests
29503247.n: 152 patients with BCLC 0 or A HCC of 4 cm or smaller randomised at four French and Swiss centres; 144 analysed per protocol, 71 patients with 98 lesions treated by microwave ablation and 73 with 104 lesions by radiofrequency ablation
29503247.bottom_line: A randomised superiority trial that failed: local tumour progression at 2 years was 6 percent of 98 lesions with microwave ablation versus 12 percent of 104 with radiofrequency ablation, risk ratio 1.62 (95% CI 0.66 to 3.94), p = 0.27, with no difference in residual tumour, time to progression, survival or complications. Because it was designed to detect an implausibly large difference, the null result does not establish that the two techniques are equivalent, and the trial never tested the 3 to 4 cm lesions in which microwave ablation is supposed to help.
29503247.funding: Grant from Microsulis (AngioDynamics), the manufacturer of the microwave device, which also funded editing support; the sponsor reviewed the submitted manuscript; the authors declare no competing interests

limitations: Open-label design without blinded response assessment, which the authors state was not feasible because imaging appearances differ after the two treatments
A hepatitis B-predominant population, which the authors acknowledge limits generalisability
critique: Median time to progression on sorafenib was only 11.7 weeks, shorter than in either pivotal sorafenib trial, so the control arm may have underperformed; 84.4 percent of patients had hepatitis B, a group in which sorafenib outcomes are less favourable

Overall survival is a secondary endpoint whose upper confidence limit reaches 0.98, and 90.7 percent of the sorafenib arm crossed over to chemoembolisation plus radiotherapy within 24 weeks, so the survival comparison contrasts immediate with deferred locoregional therapy rather than two treatments

The primary endpoint is a 12-week progression-free survival rate, a short-term surrogate, assessed open-label by the treating centre in a comparison where the post-treatment appearances differ systematically between arms

The proportion of patients with cirrhosis is never reported, which is the variable that determines whether repeated chemoembolisation plus 45 Gy is safe in another unit's hands, as the accompanying commentary points out

The protocol is hard to export: cisplatin-based chemoembolisation on a fixed 6-week schedule with gelatin sponge omitted at operator discretion, a median of four sessions in 24 weeks, and a median of 40 Gy in 2.5 to 3.0 Gy fractions by 3D-conformal technique rather than contemporary stereotactic radiotherapy

The intervention is a two-component regimen and the trial cannot say what each contributes, so the result cannot be read as evidence for radiotherapy or for chemoembolisation separately in portal vein invasion

Ninety patients at one centre in a population with a median tumour of 9.7 cm and multifocal disease in 79 percent is too small to support the aggressive strategy the trial advocates for patients whose liver is already heavily burdened
The comparator is no longer first-line, so the trial cannot address whether this regimen should be added to or substituted for an immunotherapy combination in macrovascular invasion

Patients with main portal vein invasion and preserved flow only on one side were eligible, so the irradiated volume and the embolised territory varied with anatomy in ways the paper does not relate to outcome
29543938.n: 90 treatment-naive patients with liver-confined HCC invading at least the first- or second-branch portal vein with preserved unilateral portal flow, Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0 to 1, randomised 1:1 at Asan Medical Center, Seoul between July 2013 and October 2016 to sorafenib (45) or chemoembolisation every 6 weeks plus 3D-conformal radiotherapy to the vascular invasion (45); median maximal tumour diameter was 9.7 cm, 78.9 percent had multiple lesions and 84.4 percent had hepatitis B
29543938.bottom_line: A single-centre randomised trial showing that chemoembolisation plus conformal radiotherapy to the portal invasion beats sorafenib on 12-week progression-free survival (86.7 against 34.3 percent) and on median overall survival (55.0 against 43.0 weeks). The primary endpoint is a 12-week surrogate judged without blinding, 90.7 percent of the sorafenib arm crossed over within 24 weeks so the survival comparison is of two sequences, and the sorafenib arm underperformed its own historical benchmarks.
29543938.funding: Publicly and institutionally funded; one author declares advisory and research funding from Bayer, the manufacturer of the comparator drug, and from Gilead

limitations: Patients with Child-Pugh class B or worse liver function and poorer performance status were excluded, and the authors state that further studies are needed to establish safety and efficacy in them

The authors report that the hazard ratio for death was 0.69 in hepatitis B-related and 1.11 in hepatitis C-related disease, and 0.86 in patients of Asian race but 1.01 in patients enrolled in Asia, and state that further analyses are needed to understand these differences

The authors note that hazard ratios in subgroups can be distorted by small numbers, imbalances in prognostic factors or differences in subsequent therapy, and that subgroup confidence intervals are descriptive with no adjustment for multiplicity
Dose reductions occurred in the majority of patients and the median average daily dose was 35.8 mg, which the authors compare with the 43 mg delivered in the renal-cell carcinoma trial
The authors state that the population studied represents a small percentage of patients with HCC
critique: The intention-to-treat population is defined by a data cutoff rather than by randomisation: 773 patients were randomised by September 2017 but only the 707 randomised before 1 June 2017 are analysed, so 66 randomised patients appear in no efficacy analysis of a trial described as intention to treat

The effect estimate shrank between the two looks, from a hazard ratio of 0.71 at 321 deaths to 0.76 at 484 deaths, which is the expected pattern when a trial is stopped at the first boundary crossing and means the published 0.76 is more likely an overestimate than an underestimate of the true effect

The protocol specified that no further analysis of overall survival would be performed once the null was rejected at an interim look, so the trial was designed in a way that guarantees the prespecified final estimate at 621 deaths can never exist

Placebo median progression-free survival was 1.9 months with a 95 percent confidence interval of 1.9 to 1.9, which is the first scheduled 8-week scan, so the progression-free survival hazard ratio of 0.44 is substantially an artefact of the assessment schedule rather than a measure of disease control

Progression and response were assessed by the investigator with no blinded independent central review, and an objective response rate of 4 percent (18 partial responses) against under 1 percent means the progression-free survival advantage consists almost entirely of stable disease on serial imaging
The subgroup whose only previous therapy was sorafenib, with a hazard ratio of 0.70, is the figure quoted in practice, and the paper states it was not among the prespecified subgroup analyses

Treatment-related grade 5 events occurred in 6 cabozantinib patients (hepatic failure, bronchoesophageal fistula, portal vein thrombosis, upper gastrointestinal haemorrhage, pulmonary embolism and hepatorenal syndrome) against 1 on placebo, so roughly 1.3 percent of patients died of the drug against a 2.2-month median gain

Health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetic and biomarker analyses are all stated not to be reported here, so in a drug whose principal cost is toxicity the patient-reported outcomes were withheld from the publication that established its use

The entire biological rationale rests on MET and AXL, yet no patient was selected or stratified by either marker, no biomarker result is reported, and the companion MET-selected phase 3 trial of tivantinib cited in the Discussion was negative

Only 26 percent of cabozantinib and 33 percent of placebo patients received any subsequent anticancer therapy, so this is a terminal-line population with little salvage, and the control arm received placebo plus best supportive care rather than any active drug

Aetiology, a stratification factor, was recorded from case-report forms with 16 to 20 percent unknown and alcohol-related disease imbalanced at 24 against 16 percent, so the factor used to balance the randomisation was itself imprecisely captured
One patient with ECOG performance status 2 was randomised despite the eligibility requirement of 0 or 1, acknowledged only in a footnote to the baseline table

The trial sponsor collected and analysed the data, co-wrote the first draft and paid for the medical writing and editorial assistance, with no independent statistical analysis of a result that was used for registration
29972759.n: 707 patients with advanced HCC, Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0 or 1, who had progressed after at least one systemic therapy including sorafenib, randomised 2:1 at 95 centres in 19 countries and included in the 1 June 2017 interim analysis; 773 were randomised in all by September 2017, and 27 percent of those analysed had received two prior systemic regimens
29972759.bottom_line: CELESTIAL established cabozantinib as a second- or third-line option, with median overall survival 10.2 against 8.0 months (HR 0.76, 95% CI 0.63 to 0.92, p = 0.005) and progression-free survival 5.2 against 1.9 months. The result comes from the second of three planned interim analyses at 78 percent of the planned deaths, so the mature estimate will never be produced; the objective response rate was 4 percent, 68 percent had grade 3 or 4 toxicity and the median delivered dose was 35.8 mg of a 60 mg drug.
29972759.funding: Funded by Exelixis, which designed the trial with the first and last authors, was responsible with them for data collection and analysis, collaborated on the first draft and provided medical writing and editorial assistance; three authors are Exelixis employees holding company stock, and most academic authors report industry consultancy or advisory fees

limitations: Patients with Child-Pugh class B or worse cirrhosis were excluded in line with guideline recommendations for trial exclusion
Patients with an alpha-fetoprotein below 400 ng/mL were excluded on the basis of the earlier REACH result, so no further data exist for them
Only sorafenib-pretreated patients were enrolled, which the authors list as a limitation, with an expansion cohort initiated for patients given other first-line treatments
Baseline alpha-fetoprotein was the only factor with a potential imbalance between groups, which the authors attribute to chance
Health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetic and immunogenicity results are stated to be reported separately
critique: A protocol amendment on 24 April 2017, nearly two years into enrolment, removed the planned interim efficacy analysis and cut the required sample from 399 to 279 patients while reducing the assumed hazard ratio, a decision taken by the principal investigator, the steering committee and the sponsor together, and the final analysis then occurred at exactly the 221 deaths the revised design required

The design assumed a placebo median survival of 4.5 months and the observed figure was 7.3 months, so the control arm behaved quite unlike the assumption on which the revised sample size rested, and the trial cleared significance only at p = 0.0199

The enriching biomarker was unbalanced in the direction that disfavours the experimental arm (median alpha-fetoprotein 3,920 ng/mL with ramucirumab against 2,741 ng/mL with placebo, upper quartiles 20,000 against 11,861) and alpha-fetoprotein was not a stratification factor, so with only 95 control patients the trial's defining biology was left to chance

The absolute median gain is 1.2 months with an objective response rate of about 5 percent, so the benefit rests on a time-to-event endpoint in a population whose median survival remains under 9 months

The 400 ng/mL threshold is carried over from a subgroup of the negative REACH trial with no stated biological derivation, and the paper reports no VEGFR2 or other mechanistic marker linking ramucirumab's target to the benefit, so the selection is prognostic enrichment rather than demonstrated prediction

The pooled analysis of REACH-2 with REACH by a random-effects frailty model (HR 0.694) combines the confirmatory trial with the very subgroup that generated its hypothesis, so it cannot be read as independent corroboration
Response and progression were assessed locally by investigators under RECIST 1.1 with no blinded independent central review
Median follow-up for overall survival was 7.6 months against a reported median survival of 8.5 months, so half the survival estimate lies beyond the median observation period

The favourable patient-reported result is time to deterioration of the eight-item FHSI symptom index, which sits fourth in the gatekeeping sequence, while the broader quality-of-life instrument results are deferred to a separate report

The sponsor designed both the parent and the confirmatory trial, collected, analysed and interpreted the data and wrote the report, and two authors are its employees with shares and pending patents in the area

Grade 3 or worse hypertension occurred in 13 percent against 4 percent and hyponatraemia in 5 against 2 percent, so the tolerability claim that underpins the proposal to combine ramucirumab with checkpoint inhibitors is relative rather than absolute
30665869.n: 292 of 436 screened patients with advanced HCC, Child-Pugh A and a baseline alpha-fetoprotein of 400 ng/mL or more who had previously received sorafenib, randomised 2:1 to ramucirumab (197) or placebo (95) between July 2015 and August 2017; 50 patients (17 percent) had stopped sorafenib for intolerance and median prior sorafenib duration was 4.1 months
30665869.bottom_line: REACH-2 is the only positive biomarker-selected phase 3 trial in HCC, showing median overall survival of 8.5 against 7.3 months (HR 0.710, 95% CI 0.531 to 0.949, p = 0.0199) in patients with alpha-fetoprotein of 400 ng/mL or more after sorafenib. The absolute gain is 1.2 months with a 5 percent response rate, the trial's sample size and effect assumption were cut by protocol amendment after enrolment began, and the enriching biomarker was itself imbalanced between the arms it defines.
30665869.funding: Funded by Eli Lilly, which had roles in the design of both REACH and REACH-2 and in data collection, analysis, interpretation and writing of the report; two authors are Lilly employees, shareholders and hold pending patents

limitations: Single institution with an open-label design, which the authors acknowledge leaves residual bias
The subgroup analyses were not adjusted for multiple testing and may be false-positive, as the authors state
Nearly all patients had hepatitis B-related disease, which the authors note limits generalisability
Repeat hepatectomy was open, and the authors call for a comparison against laparoscopic repeat hepatectomy, which has not been studied
The authors note that a short time to recurrence is associated with recurrence arising from the original tumour rather than de novo, which they could not separate
critique: The trial was powered against a surgical result that did not exist: the calculation assumed 5-year survival of 56 percent after repeat hepatectomy and 39 percent after ablation, and the observed figures were 43.6 and 38.5 percent, so the ablation assumption was accurate and the surgical one was 12 points too optimistic

A hazard ratio of 1.26 with a confidence interval from 0.91 to 1.76 in 240 patients and 140 deaths excludes neither equivalence nor a substantial surgical advantage, yet the title, Key Points and conclusion present the result as no difference in survival

The primary endpoint is analysed six times in different populations (intention to treat p = 0.17, excluding additional anticancer treatment p = 0.24, minor hepatectomy only p = 0.20, per protocol p = 0.10, and z tests on the 5-year rates p = 0.291 and p = 0.25) with no hierarchy or multiplicity control stated

The only significant efficacy result in the paper, per-protocol 5-year repeat recurrence-free survival of 36.4 against 28.2 percent (p = 0.04), appears in a supplementary figure and is obtained by removing the crossovers and the patients lost to follow-up from an intention-to-treat comparison that gave p = 0.09

The subgroup variables were chosen from the independent risk factors identified in the trial's own multivariable model, so the variables were selected after seeing which predicted outcome in these data; no interaction test is reported, only 50 of 240 patients had a nodule above 3 cm, and a published correction was required in January 2020 to fix errors in the subgroup forest plot that carries the paper's practical message

Eligibility excluded any nodule within 1.0 cm of the gastrointestinal tract, hilum, cava, main hepatic veins, gallbladder or diaphragm, which removes every location in which ablation is known to fail, and ablation still produced nearly twice the local recurrence in that favourable anatomy

Both arms worked to a 0.5 cm margin standard, below the margin usually recommended for either technique, and 99 of 120 surgical patients had less than a bisegmentectomy, so the surgical arm is mostly limited open resection rather than anatomical re-resection

Safety is analysed as treated on 116 surgical and 124 ablation patients, different denominators from the efficacy analysis, and the surgical safety group contains one patient who received only intraoperative ablation and two who had resection plus intratumoral ethanol

Grade 3 or 4 complications were 6.0 against 1.6 percent with p = 0.09, so the severe-complication difference is not significant and the headline 22.4 against 7.3 percent is driven by Clavien-Dindo grade 1 and 2 events that the abstract reports only as a composite

The cohort is narrow in ways that remove the patients for whom the question is hardest: age capped at 60 with a median of 53, Child-Pugh A with no varices or ascites, platelets above 50 and prothrombin prolongation under 5 seconds, 90 percent male and almost entirely hepatitis B

Local repeat recurrence, the key secondary endpoint, is defined as disease within 1 cm of the ablation zone or the re-resection margin and was adjudicated by an unmasked treating team on imaging performed only every 4 to 6 months, which is also too coarse for the 12-month early-versus-late recurrence cut-point used as another secondary endpoint

Recurrence after treatment was managed at clinician discretion and 38 of 73 surgical and 51 of 77 ablation patients received multidisciplinary salvage, so overall survival reflects an unrandomised salvage pathway that was used more often in the ablation arm

Every patient had already undergone an R0 resection with no residual disease at 2 months, so the trial compares second treatments among patients already proven fit for surgery, and salvage transplantation is not considered anywhere

The trial was run at the highest-volume liver surgery unit in China with its own national liver cancer centre, so the 22.4 percent complication rate, the absence of perioperative death and the 8-day stay represent the best case for reoperation rather than a transferable estimate
31774468.n: 240 of 518 screened patients aged 20 to 60 with early-stage recurrent HCC after a previous R0 resection (solitary nodule 5 cm or less, or up to 3 nodules each 3 cm or less), randomised 1:1 at the Eastern Hepatobiliary Surgery Hospital in Shanghai between June 2010 and January 2013; 216 of 240 (90 percent) were men and 217 completed the trial
31774468.bottom_line: The only randomised comparison of repeat hepatectomy with percutaneous ablation for recurrent HCC: 5-year overall survival was 43.6 versus 38.5 percent (HR 1.26, 95% CI 0.91 to 1.76, p = 0.17) with no significant difference, but local repeat recurrence was 21.7 versus 37.8 percent and complications 22.4 versus 7.3 percent. The confidence interval admits a 76 percent higher mortality with ablation, the two subgroup findings the paper is cited for are unadjusted and rest on 50 patients with a nodule above 3 cm, and the eligibility rules excluded every anatomical site where ablation fails.
31774468.funding: Government-funded; the authors declare no conflicts of interest

limitations: Open-label design, chosen to spare patients two placebo infusions, which the authors list as a limitation although blinded independent review protected the progression-free survival endpoint
Enrolment was restricted to Child-Pugh A patients who had been screened and treated for varices, so the authors state that the safety of the combination in a broader population needs further study
The authors note that no biomarker has been shown to predict benefit in HCC and that work is needed to identify who benefits
The authors state that survival data were not yet mature at this analysis
critique: The primary survival analysis is the first interim look at 161 of 312 planned deaths (52 percent) with a median follow-up of 8.6 months, and the 12-month landmark survival rates of 67.2 and 54.6 percent are therefore estimated beyond the median duration of follow-up in either arm

Dose modification was not permitted for atezolizumab or bevacizumab but was permitted for sorafenib, and patients who stopped one component of the combination could continue the other, so the experimental regimen was a flexible strategy while the control was a fixed comparator, and attrition for toxicity falls differently in the two arms by design
Both arms could continue treatment beyond radiographic progression at the investigator's judgment of clinical benefit, a decision made without masking in a trial whose primary endpoint is survival

The 2:1 allocation leaves 165 control patients with 65 deaths, so every comparison rests on an imprecisely estimated sorafenib arm, and the stratified analyses dropped ECOG performance status from the stratification factors used in analysis despite its being a randomisation stratum, with no explanation

Every patient underwent screening endoscopy with all varices treated to local standard before entry, and 26 percent had varices with 11 to 14 percent treated, so the trial pre-selected and pre-treated exactly the bleeding risk that bevacizumab exacerbates, and its bleeding rates cannot be read outside that protocol
Diagnosis could be made on clinical and imaging criteria without tissue, and 2 to 4 percent of patients were BCLC stage A, so a minority of a first-line systemic therapy trial had early-stage disease

Patient-reported quality of life, physical functioning and role functioning were secondary endpoints defined on a 10-point EORTC change and collected by self-report in an unmasked trial, which is the circumstance in which such endpoints are least interpretable

No biomarker selection or biomarker result is reported although atezolizumab is a PD-L1 inhibitor with companion diagnostics in other tumours, so there is no way to identify the roughly one patient in four who responds

Hepatitis B accounted for 49 percent of patients and 40 percent came from Asia excluding Japan, while non-viral disease, which dominates Western practice, was only 30 percent and would later show no survival benefit in the trial's own updated subgroup analysis

The sponsor supplied the drugs and collaborated on the design, collection, analysis and interpretation of the data, employed six authors and funded the editorial assistance, with no independently conducted analysis of the registration result
The article carries a notice that it was updated on 19 May 2020, five days after publication, without the content of the correction being stated in the text
32402160.n: 501 patients with locally advanced, metastatic or unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0 or 1 and no previous systemic therapy, randomised 2:1 to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab (336) or sorafenib (165) at 111 sites in 17 countries between March 2018 and January 2019; 49 percent had hepatitis B and 30 percent non-viral disease
32402160.bottom_line: IMbrave150 displaced sorafenib as first-line therapy, reporting a hazard ratio for death of 0.58 (95% CI 0.42 to 0.79) with 12-month survival of 67.2 against 54.6 percent and median progression-free survival of 6.8 against 4.3 months. The analysis is the first of two planned interim looks at 161 of 312 planned deaths with a median follow-up of 8.6 months, so no median survival could be estimated for the combination; entry required endoscopy with all varices treated, and dose modification was permitted for sorafenib but not for the experimental regimen.
32402160.funding: Funded by F. Hoffmann-La Roche/Genentech, which provided the trial drugs and collaborated with an academic steering committee on design and on the collection, analysis and interpretation of the data; six of the 22 authors are sponsor employees and editorial assistance was sponsor-funded

limitations: A national change in graft allocation policy and HCC priorities during accrual forced the trial to close at 45 of the planned 260 patients, which the authors state limits the strength of the conclusion
The authors acknowledge heterogeneity of the applied downstaging protocols, since therapy and schedule were centre-based and unrestricted
The authors state that predictability of downstaging success was beyond the scope of the study and would need specific protocols, particularly in hepatitis C
Explant pathology showed a tendency to tumour re-growth even after radiological complete response, which the authors report and attribute to the time to transplantation

The authors note that transarterial chemoembolisation rarely achieves cure despite radiological complete response, since only 2 of the 4 non-recurring controls were cured and both had ablation or resection
The subgroup difference in survival benefit between partial and complete responders is reported by the authors as not significant at the 5 percent level (p for interaction 0.105)
critique: The conditional power of 98.6 percent is a projection, not evidence: it is the probability that significance would persist if the observed HR of 0.22 attenuated only to the planned 0.50 across a hypothetical further 215 patients, so it assumes the answer and cannot substitute for the 65 deaths that were never observed

The 2 patients randomised to transplantation who refused it are described as censored in the intervention group according to the intention-to-treat principle, but censoring is not intention to treat: both progressed and died at 17 and 20 months, and removing those deaths from the transplant arm inflates the only outcome the trial reports

Survival is counted from randomisation, so the 29 of 74 enrolled patients (39 percent) who never reached randomisation, including 22 progressions and 2 deaths during downstaging, appear in no survival analysis; the trial reports no outcome for the downstaging strategy as a whole, which is the question a clinician faces at presentation

The control arm was treated only at the time of progression, while standard care for intermediate-stage HCC is continued locoregional therapy; the comparison is therefore transplantation versus deferred salvage rather than transplantation versus best available therapy, and best available therapy in 2011 to 2015 meant sorafenib

Randomisation did not balance the key prognostic variable: residual tumour burden was significantly higher in the transplant arm (p = 0.03) and 9 percent of the transplant arm versus none of the controls were beyond Milan criteria at randomisation, in 45 patients with no adjustment for either

Explant pathology in the 23 transplant-arm patients showed tumour burden returning from a median of 0 at randomisation to a median of 4.8 (range 0 to 9.6), close to the enrolment median of 7.3, so most grafts went to tumours that were no longer within the criteria the randomisation was based on; the paper reports this as a non-significant trend (p = 0.158)

Two of the 5 deaths in the transplant arm occurred within 30 days (myocardial infarction on day 10, multiorgan failure on day 20), a 30-day mortality of 2 of 21 transplanted patients, which is never stated as an operative mortality figure in a trial whose purpose is to justify consuming grafts

The eligibility ceiling was a Metroticket prediction of at least 50 percent 5-year survival, a calculator derived by the senior author from a retrospective series and never validated for prospective patient selection, so the entry criterion is the investigators' own model

Randomisation was stratified by compliance with sorafenib during downstaging, but sorafenib was non-mandatory and 24 of 54 patients (44 percent) stopped it for intolerance or worsening liver function, so the stratification variable was unstable and the trial has no way to separate the contribution of sorafenib from that of the locoregional treatments

The co-primary tumour endpoint composites two different events measured differently in the two arms, recurrence after transplantation against progression of residual disease in controls, in an open-label trial with no blinded central imaging review

The policy proposal in the Discussion, that partially responding tumours be prioritised on the waiting list, rests on a subgroup contrast of 26.5 versus 9.9 months in mean survival benefit whose confidence interval for complete responders crosses zero (-5.5 to 25.3) and whose interaction p value is 0.105

Two different p values are printed for the same primary comparison, p = 0.004 for the Cox hazard ratio in the abstract and log-rank p = 0.002 in the Discussion, and the Discussion restates the effect inverted as HR 4.50 without saying so

There was no provision for a formal interim analysis, yet the trial was closed early on the monitoring committee's recommendation and then analysed after four further years of follow-up with the data already in hand, and no alpha adjustment is made for either the data-dependent stopping or the data-dependent analysis time

The grafts used were not of high quality (median donor age 69 years, range 18 to 84; median D-MELD 594; macrosteatosis of 10 percent or more in 8 of 22 livers) and the trial's own framing is the optimal use of a scarce resource, yet no analysis of what the 21 grafts cost non-cancer candidates is presented

The authors declare no competing interests, but the senior author wrote the Italian allocation consensus the trial cites, both Metroticket models used for eligibility and prognostication, and the adaptive-allocation proposal the conclusions advance; no intellectual conflict is disclosed
32615109.n: 74 patients with HCC beyond Milan criteria and at least 50 percent predicted 5-year post-transplant survival on the Metroticket calculator enrolled at 9 Italian centres between March 2011 and March 2015; 54 (73 percent) were successfully downstaged and 45 randomised, 23 to transplantation (21 actually transplanted) and 22 to non-transplant therapy
32615109.bottom_line: The only randomised trial of transplantation after downstaging: among 45 patients with a sustained mRECIST response, 5-year overall survival was 77.5 percent with transplantation versus 31.2 percent with continued non-transplant therapy (HR 0.22, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.61), a mean survival gain of 14.5 months. It was stopped at 45 of 260 planned patients with 21 of 87 planned deaths, the control arm received only sorafenib-era therapy and was treated only on progression, and explant pathology showed tumour burden back near baseline, so it shows that a graft beats 2011-2015 palliation in a highly selected 61 percent of enrolled patients rather than that downstaging identifies favourable biology.
32615109.funding: Investigator-initiated, funded by the Italian Ministry of Health (Finalized Research Program in Oncology RF-INT-2006-394471) and endorsed by AISF, the North Italian Transplant programme and the Italian National Transplant Centre; no industry support was requested; the authors declare no competing interests

limitations: Small sample resulting from early stopping for efficacy at the planned interim analysis
Macroaggregated albumin scintigraphy was used as a surrogate for microsphere distribution
Generalisability to lesions smaller than 7 cm and to resin microspheres at 100 to 120 Gy is untested, which the authors state
critique: The trial was stopped at the planned interim analysis for efficacy and the survival difference is a secondary endpoint resting on 14 deaths in the personalised arm, so a 16-month median gain from 60 randomised patients is almost certainly an overestimate of the true effect

The primary endpoint was unmasked, investigator-read EASL response of a single index lesion at 3 months, which says nothing about the rest of the liver, and progression-free survival, the harder endpoint, did not differ significantly between the arms

Ten of 28 patients in the personalised arm went on to curative resection against one in the standard arm, so part of the survival difference is surgery rather than radiation, and although the difference persisted after post hoc censoring at the date of surgery, that censoring was not prespecified

Eligibility selected heavily for a result: an index lesion of 7 cm or more, at least 30 percent hepatic reserve preserved, satisfactory mapping and randomisation only after the scintigraphy, so patients whose anatomy would not permit personalised dosing never entered

Safety was analysed by the treatment actually received on central dosimetry rather than as randomised, so 8 patients randomised to standard dosimetry were reclassified, and some of the percentages in the safety table are internally inconsistent
The dose threshold of 205 Gy to the index lesion is applied as the intervention in the same trial that advances it, so the number is not independently derived

The control arm used 120 plus or minus 20 Gy to the perfused lobe, which the trial then shows to be inadequate, so the comparison is between a dose chosen to work and a dose the investigators already believed was too low
The device manufacturer funded the trial, validated the study design and paid for the editorial assistance, and the result supports its product's dosing approach
33166497.n: 60 patients with unresectable locally advanced HCC, an index lesion of 7 cm or more, at least 30 percent hepatic reserve after treatment and no extrahepatic spread, randomised 1:1 at four French centres between December 2015 and January 2018 after mapping scintigraphy to personalised dosimetry (31) or standard dosimetry (29); 56 were treated, 89 percent were BCLC C and 70 percent had portal vein invasion
33166497.bottom_line: DOSISPHERE-01 is the trial that showed dose matters: targeting at least 205 Gy to the index lesion gave an objective response of 71 against 36 percent and median survival of 26.6 against 10.7 months compared with standard 120 Gy lobar dosimetry. It is a 60-patient phase 2 trial stopped early for efficacy with an unmasked single-lesion response endpoint, no significant difference in progression-free survival, and ten patients in the personalised arm going on to resection against one in the control arm.
33166497.funding: Funded by Biocompatibles UK, a Boston Scientific company and the maker of the TheraSphere glass microspheres used, which validated the study design and funded editorial assistance; the first author and most senior authors report grants or personal fees from the sponsor

limitations: Retrospective design, lack of a control arm and limited sample size compared with systemic therapy trials, all stated by the authors

The authors state that overall survival could have been a primary endpoint but that BCLC A studies are difficult because of the long natural history and effective post-progression treatments, so a surrogate was used
The authors note that 39.5 percent of patients were classed BCLC C only because of an ECOG score of 1 from cancer-related symptoms
critique: The primary endpoint, localised mRECIST, scores only the treated zone, which near-guarantees a high figure for an ablative segmental dose; the same patients show 46.3 percent confirmed response by RECIST 1.1, so the headline number is a property of the metric as much as of the treatment

Twenty-eight percent of patients went on to transplantation or resection, so the 3-year survival of 86.6 percent cannot be attributed to radioembolisation and the paper reports no analysis censoring or excluding those patients

The population is selected on every axis that favours the result: solitary tumour, Child-Pugh A only, no prior therapy, no vascular invasion, median diameter 2.7 cm and nearly two thirds under 3 cm, which is the size range in which thermal ablation is already curative

The 400 Gy threshold dose the paper proposes for an ablative effect comes from a subset dose-pathology correlation within this same uncontrolled cohort, so a dose threshold is derived and endorsed in the series that generated it

Two of the reported figures are internally impossible as printed, a median progression-free survival given as 57.9 percent with a confidence interval of 40.7 to 57.9 and a median overall survival given as reached at 57.9 with a confidence interval of not estimable to not estimable

The Discussion imports the DOSISPHERE-01 survival figures of 26.6 against 10.7 months to argue for personalised dosimetry, which belong to a different trial in locally advanced disease and not to this cohort

A single-arm retrospective series became the basis of a premarket approval, so the device's approved indication rests on a design that cannot compare it with ablation, resection or chemoembolisation in the same patients

The sponsor funded the study and supplied the statistical support, scientific input, trial management and medical writing, two authors are its employees holding stock, and the independent central review and auditing the paper offers as strengths were commissioned within that arrangement

Eighteen percent of patients were over 75 and 39.5 percent were labelled BCLC C on performance status alone, so the cohort mixes patients whose staging reflects symptoms rather than tumour extent with the very early tumours that drive the response rate
33739462.n: 162 consecutive patients with a solitary HCC of 8 cm or less and Child-Pugh A cirrhosis treated with Y-90 glass microspheres at three US centres between January 2014 and December 2017; median tumour diameter 2.7 cm with 62 percent under 3 cm, median absorbed dose 410 Gy, and 45 patients (28 percent) subsequently transplanted or resected
33739462.bottom_line: LEGACY is the retrospective single-arm series that supported FDA premarket approval of TheraSphere for solitary unresectable HCC, reporting an 88.3 percent objective response by localised mRECIST with 62.2 percent lasting at least 6 months and 3-year survival of 86.6 percent. It has no comparator, the primary endpoint scores only the treated zone and falls to 46.3 percent by RECIST 1.1, and 28 percent of patients went on to transplantation or resection.
33739462.funding: Funded by Boston Scientific, which also supplied statistical support, scientific input, trial management and medical writing; two authors are company employees holding stock and most other authors consult for the sponsor

limitations: Short post-transplant follow-up in a relatively small number of transplanted patients; the authors state it will take another 2 to 3 years to report the survival and recurrence data that would confirm efficacy
Three of the ten intended centres from two further UNOS regions could not supply data and were removed from the consortium, reducing power and applicability
The study was performed before the median-MELD-at-transplant-minus-3 allocation rule, so it cannot describe current waiting-list behaviour or access
Referral bias is possible because patients treated with locoregional therapy in the community who then progressed may never have been referred for transplantation
Centre-specific differences in the choice of first locoregional therapy persisted, ranging from 36 to 90 percent chemoembolisation across the 7 centres
Not all patients had AFP-L3, des-gamma-carboxyprothrombin or neutrophil-lymphocyte ratio measured at baseline, which the authors state limits the biomarker analysis
The authors concede that down-staging to within Milan criteria should be regarded as only a minimum requirement, given the under-staging rate
critique: The study population is conditional on transplant candidacy, not on tumour burden: 115 of 324 patients (35.5 percent) with eligible tumours were excluded for medical or psychosocial contraindications, decompensation with AFP above 1000 ng/mL, or bilirubin above 4, so the 83 percent success rate does not describe the patients a tumour board would consider for down-staging

Patients removed from the protocol for a non-liver medical contraindication, loss of interest or non-compliance were censored at delisting rather than counted as failures, so the analysis called intention-to-treat does not include the commonest competing routes out of the pathway

mRECIST response was assessed a median of 4.3 weeks after chemoembolisation but 6.3 weeks after Y-90 (p = 0.03), and radiation response is known to be delayed, so the central claim that the two treatments produced similar response compares measurements made at systematically different times

The chemoembolisation-versus-Y-90 comparison is non-randomised with large baseline imbalance (male 92.4 versus 72.6 percent, p < 0.001; multifocal disease 75.8 versus 51.6 percent, p = 0.003; MELD p = 0.04) and the choice was driven by centre (p = 0.001), yet every comparison is reported as an unadjusted p value and interpreted as no difference

The explant comparison that most favours Y-90 rests on 13 explants: 4 of 13 completely necrotic and 3 of 13 beyond Milan criteria against 9 of 44 and 19 of 44 for chemoembolisation, differences the paper describes in the Discussion while reporting p values of 0.44 and 0.76
15 patients (7.2 percent) received some other first locoregional therapy and are silently dropped, so the comparison covers 194 of 209 patients without the omission being stated

HCC was never confirmed by biopsy at any of the seven institutions and nodules under 1 cm were not counted, so both the entry tumour burden and the down-staging endpoint rest on imaging in a study whose headline result is that imaging understaged 42.8 percent of explants

AFP-L3 of 10 percent or more, the only independent dropout predictor, was measured in 83 of 209 patients (40 percent) and yields a sub-hazard ratio of 3.7 with a confidence interval from 1.27 to 10.79 from a model containing two covariates, selected from univariable screening at p < 0.1

Nearly half the cohort came from two centres (68 patients, 32.5 percent, and 33 patients, 15.8 percent), and no model in the paper includes a centre-level random effect or fixed effect despite demonstrated centre-driven treatment choice

43.2 percent of the dropouts for tumour progression occurred during the mandatory 6-month wait before MELD exception points, so nearly half the progression events happened before the patient could be prioritised; the paper treats the waiting rule as biological selection rather than as an access barrier that the data could quantify

The abstract reports dropout as 37.3 percent and the Results as 35.9 percent without explaining that the first is the 2-year competing-risk estimate and the second the crude proportion, and the two figures are used interchangeably in the Discussion
Post-transplant survival of 100 percent at 1 year and 95 percent at 2 years falls to 83.1 percent by 3 years in the same 63 patients, and the abstract and lay summary quote only the 2-year figure

The study is presented as validating the UNOS policy, but the protocol being validated is the authors' own UCSF and Region 5 protocol that UNOS adopted, the validation was done by the same group at seven experienced high-volume centres, and the prognostic score used as the benchmark (RETREAT) is also the first author's

The first and senior authors hold advisory roles and institutional research funding from Wako Diagnostics, whose assays measure AFP-L3 and des-gamma-carboxyprothrombin, the two biomarkers the paper advances as candidates for selection
34331914.n: 209 consecutive patients meeting UNOS down-staging eligibility criteria at 7 US transplant centres in 4 UNOS regions, enrolled 2016 to 2019 from 324 with eligible tumour burden; 174 were successfully down-staged, 75 dropped out and 63 reached transplantation
34331914.bottom_line: The first prospective multiregional test of the UNOS down-staging protocol: 83 percent of 209 patients were down-staged to within Milan criteria, 2-year cumulative dropout was 37.3 percent, 46.6 percent reached transplantation by 3 years and 2-year post-transplant survival was 95 percent, with no detectable difference between chemoembolisation and Y-90. The finding that matters is the 42.8 percent of explants beyond Milan criteria, which shows that imaging-defined down-staging does not reliably identify the tumour it claims to; post-transplant follow-up was a median 1.7 years in 63 patients, and the TACE-versus-Y-90 comparison is unadjusted and confounded.
34331914.funding: Supported in part by a National Institutes of Health grant to the UCSF Liver Center (P30 DK026743); the first author reports advisory boards for and institutional research funding from Wako Diagnostics plus funding from Glycotest and Target PharmaSolutions, the senior author institutional funding from Wako Diagnostics, and two further authors multiple industry relationships

limitations: The evidence review closed in February 2020, so a Korean randomised trial of proton therapy versus radiofrequency ablation for recurrent HCC and a completed randomised trial of EBRT after incomplete TAE or TACE appeared too late to be assessed; the task force says so explicitly.

No published randomised trial compares EBRT with thermal ablation or with catheter-based therapy for liver-confined HCC. The task force names the main limitations of the studies it relied on as the absence of randomised data, the paucity of direct comparison with systemic or other therapies, and selection bias between treatment groups in observational designs.

The literature search was restricted to studies in which EBRT formed part of the treatment, so outcome data on non-EBRT liver-directed therapies were limited; a supplementary search of meta-analyses and systematic reviews was run but, by the task force's own account, heterogeneity in populations, tumour characteristics and outcome metrics meant it did not provide meaningful comparative data, and it was kept out of the evidence tables.

Supporting studies largely excluded Child-Pugh B8 or worse disease, and in the best prospective dose study 50% of Child-Pugh A patients progressed to a higher Child-Pugh class and 33% of Child-Pugh B patients to class C.

Technique, dose-constraint and motion-management recommendations combine evidence with expert opinion. Whether protons are better than photons is unresolved pending NRG GI-003 (NCT03186898), and the single-institution retrospective comparison that favoured protons is conceded to be insufficient to recommend one modality over another.

The task force states the guideline is not a substitute for multidisciplinary evaluation and discussion, and that future studies should further define the role of EBRT in the context of liver-directed and systemic therapies.
critique: ASTRO's own grading table permits a Strong recommendation at any quality of evidence, listed as 'usually high, moderate, or expert opinion', so the Strong first-line recommendation for EBRT carries no guarantee that randomised data lie behind it. A reader who treats 'strong recommendation' as a statement about evidence is being misled by the grading scheme rather than by the prose.

Consensus is assessed by a confidential modified Delphi on a five-point Likert scale with a threshold of 75% agreement, or 90% for expert-opinion recommendations, and recommendations failing the threshold are 'removed or revised'. No agreement percentage is printed for any recommendation in the document, so the reader cannot distinguish a unanimous recommendation from one that just cleared 75%, and cannot see what was dropped.

The Society of Interventional Radiology participated early and then withdrew as a collaborating society during development, a fact disclosed only in the acknowledgements. The withdrawn society is the one that delivers the TACE and TARE against which EBRT is being positioned, so the comparator specialty is absent from a guideline that recommends sequencing with and substituting for its treatments.

The task force is drawn almost entirely from radiation oncology, with single representatives from surgical oncology, transplant surgery and medical oncology. A guideline making a modality first-line is written predominantly by the specialty that delivers it, and surgical oncologists published a dissenting 'surgical perspective' in Annals of Surgical Oncology the following year; that commentary is identified here from its citation and abstract and was not obtained in full.

The first-line recommendation converts an absence of comparison into a permission. EBRT is recommended for patients with liver-confined HCC 'who are not candidates for curative therapy', and the guideline supplies no criteria for who is not a candidate, so the boundary between the recommended population and patients who should have resection, ablation or transplantation is set by whoever applies it.

Cost, access and equipment availability appear nowhere; the word cost does not occur in the document. Recommendations that rest on proton therapy and on motion-managed ultrahypofractionated delivery presuppose technology concentrated in a few centres, and the guideline addresses a reader with neither only by saying the choice should reflect 'available technology'.

HCC and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma are handled in one document under shared key questions despite different natural history, systemic options and surgical pathways. The dose and constraint tables serve both diseases, and the bolded regimens in them are identified as the most common prescriptions 'based on consensus of the task force' rather than derived from dose-response data.

Hepatic toxicity is reported as change in Child-Pugh class rather than as decompensating events, hospital admissions or deaths, so the figures cited (50% of Child-Pugh A patients rising a class, 33% of Child-Pugh B patients reaching C) cannot be set against the complication rates reported for ablation or embolisation, and no numerical risk of radiation-induced liver disease is attached to any recommended regimen.

The adjuvant recommendation for resected intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma is extrapolated from SWOG S0809, a single-arm phase 2 study of postoperative chemoradiation in extrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma that explicitly excluded intrahepatic disease. The task force recommends on the stated grounds that the clinical context and nodal target volumes are similar.

Biologically effective dose is tabulated throughout on an assumed alpha-beta ratio of 10, applied unchanged across standard fractionation, moderate hypofractionation and ultrahypofractionation. The equivalence between the listed regimens depends entirely on that single assumed value and no sensitivity to it is shown.
34688956.bottom_line: Establishes a graded, multidisciplinary framework for where external beam radiotherapy fits in HCC and intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, with dose, fractionation and organ-at-risk tables a radiation oncologist can work from, and makes EBRT a named first-line option for liver-confined HCC when curative treatment is not available. It does not establish that EBRT is equivalent or preferable to ablation, embolisation or surgery, because no randomised comparison with any of them existed at the February 2020 search cut-off and the grading scheme permits a Strong recommendation to rest on expert opinion. Read it as radiation oncology's consensus on how to deliver EBRT well, not as evidence on whether to choose it.
34688956.funding: Funded by the American Society for Radiation Oncology, which states it develops and publishes guidelines without commercial support and that task force members volunteer their time; individual disclosures are printed, including the vice chair's honoraria and consultancy from Medtronic and members' relationships with Varian, Elekta, General Electric, Philips, Boston Scientific, Blueprint Medicines and Eli Lilly, while the chair and five other members report none

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that no portal pressure cut-off can be given for resection in the presence of clinically significant portal hypertension, that robust cut-offs are likewise lacking for the BCLC B subdivision, that the LEGACY cohort supporting radioembolisation for single nodules up to 8 cm awaits external validation, that there is no evidence base for sequencing after a first-line immunotherapy doublet, and, in general terms, that data for some encouraging interventions are still too immature to be incorporated into an evidence-based model and that observational studies have limitations for robust causal inference.
critique: This is an expert narrative review, not a systematically reviewed or GRADE-graded guideline. No search strategy, inclusion criteria, evidence tables or voting procedure are reported, so the reader cannot establish which literature was considered or how the recommendations in Figure 1 were reached.

The author contribution statement records that initial and final writing of the manuscript was by two authors, with the remaining sixteen contributing 'critical reading and suggestions'. The document carries the authority of an eighteen-author international panel while having been drafted by the two senior figures of the group whose system it is.

The new liver-function layer is introduced without thresholds. ALBI, AFP, MELD and ascites grade are named as inputs to patient characterisation and no cut-off is given for any of them, so two boards can apply BCLC 2022 to the same patient, assign different stages and different treatments, and both be following the algorithm; a correspondence in the same journal made exactly this point.

Treatment stage migration is central to the model and has no rule. The document says when to consider migrating a patient to the treatment of an adjacent stage but gives no criterion for doing it, which places the most consequential judgement in the algorithm outside the algorithm.

The radioembolisation recommendation for single nodules up to 8 cm rests on LEGACY, one retrospective single-arm cohort whose median tumour size was 2.6 cm. The upper bound of the recommendation is three times the median of the series that generated it, and nothing in the figure signals that the evidence thins across that range.

Resection is not recommended for multinodular disease or in the presence of clinically significant portal hypertension, and surgeons wrote to the journal to say the model stays too restrictive and accommodates neither bile duct tumour thrombus nor the distinction between tumour-related and comorbidity-related performance status. The exchange, including the authors' reply, is identified here from the citations and abstracts and was not obtained in full.

External beam radiotherapy, stereotactic body radiotherapy included, is absent from the algorithm, and radiation oncologists published a correspondence saying so within months. Omitting a modality in routine use is a positive claim about its place, made here by silence rather than argument, and the same group reversed the position in its 2026 update.

The figure is the product. Most readers will use Figure 1 alone and a figure cannot carry the qualifications the text attaches to it, so the caveats that make the recommendations defensible are separated from the thing that gets applied. The 2023 AASLD guidance reproduces this figure as its own Figure 9, carrying the algorithm into a second document without the text that qualifies it.

The evidence cut-off is 15 November 2021, so the document neither addresses adjuvant systemic therapy nor considers TACE combined with systemic therapy. It continued to be cited and reproduced as current for years, and nothing in it states an expiry or an update interval.

BCLC D survival is given as around three months, a figure the same group revised to under twelve months in 2026 on data largely available earlier. For a stage where the quoted prognosis is itself part of the decision to treat or not, a fourfold revision between editions means the 2022 figure was shaping choices it could not support.
34801630.bottom_line: Establishes the 2022 version of the staging and treatment algorithm most of the world uses for HCC, adds a liver-function and patient-characterisation layer above tumour burden, and brings radioembolisation in for single nodules up to 8 cm. It does not establish any of this systematically: it is an expert narrative review drafted by two of its eighteen authors, with no search strategy, no voting, no thresholds for the liver-function variables it introduces, and no rule for the treatment stage migration on which the model depends. Use it as the field's shared vocabulary, and read the published correspondence from radiation oncologists, surgeons and hepatologists as part of the document.
34801630.funding: No commercial funding; the authors' research is partially supported by Instituto de Salud Carlos III, the Spanish Health Ministry's National Strategic Plan against Hepatitis C, AECC, CIBERehd, an EASL grant, NIH R01 MD012565 and Horizon 2020 grant agreement 952103. limitations: No limitations section; the faculty concede only that COVID-19 forced the workshop to be postponed and held virtually rather than face to face and call this a limitation, that the non-invasive thresholds are unestablished in obese NASH, in primary biliary cholangitis where a pre-sinusoidal component makes HVPG underestimate portal hypertension, and in other aetiologies, that in NASH cirrhosis clinical signs of portal hypertension can be present with an HVPG below 10 mmHg (statement 1.12, evidence level C.2), and, in the research agenda, that the prognostic role of HVPG before surgery needs prospective study against non-invasive tests and that non-invasive tools for clinically significant portal hypertension need validation in NASH and other aetiologies.
critique: The disclosure is not credible as written. Participants declared nothing to disclose regarding funding while the same document thanks EASL, AASLD and eight other bodies for the unrestricted grants that paid for the meeting, and three authors declare company relationships a few pages earlier. The declaration appears to cover the manuscript rather than the conference and the document does not say which.

The statement an HCC board needs most is the one without a number. Statement 1.18 makes clinically significant portal hypertension an A.1 risk marker for decompensation and death after resection for HCC and names no HVPG or liver stiffness threshold at which resection should be declined, so it identifies a contraindication-shaped risk without defining the contraindication.

A single HVPG definition of 10 mmHg is applied across aetiologies the document itself says behave differently. Statement 1.12 concedes at evidence level C.2 that in NASH cirrhosis clinical signs of portal hypertension occur below 10 mmHg, so the threshold does not mean the same thing across the aetiology mix a Western hepatobiliary practice now sees, and no alternative is offered.

The grey zone between the rule-out (liver stiffness 15 kPa or less with platelets 150 x 10^9/L or more) and the rule-in (25 kPa or more) is handled by ANTICIPATE at a 60% probability of clinically significant portal hypertension, as a weak B.2 recommendation. Sixty per cent is not a decision threshold for something as irreversible as declining resection, and the band it covers is wide: 20 to 25 kPa with platelets under 150, or 15 to 20 kPa with platelets under 110.

Thresholds are given to the kilopascal without the measurement conditions that generate them. Vibration-controlled transient elastography values vary with fasting state, operator, probe and hepatic inflammation, and no statement reports the variability around a single measurement or requires a repeat before a 15 or 25 kPa value is acted on.

Evidence grades are assigned per statement but the studies behind them are not tabulated, and the document is 12,632 words of statements with the derivations left in the narrative. For the surgically decisive statements this means a reader cannot see how many patients, in which aetiologies, support a given kilopascal value.

Baveno VII sits awkwardly beside BCLC and EASL guidance, which treat clinically significant portal hypertension as effectively excluding resection, and it does not address the conflict. A later randomised trial reported equivalent survival after resection versus ablation or TACE in hepatitis B-related HCC with clinically significant portal hypertension, which is the study the research agenda asked for and which cuts against how the marker is used.

Patients starting atezolizumab plus bevacizumab are not covered. Bevacizumab carries a bleeding risk and these patients have portal hypertension by definition, yet no statement addresses variceal screening or prophylaxis before systemic therapy. A letter in the Journal of Hepatology made this point within months; that letter is identified here from its citation and title and was not obtained in full.

Pre-sinusoidal disease defeats the whole framework and is handled in a clause. Where HVPG underestimates portal pressure, as in primary biliary cholangitis, the reference standard and the non-invasive tests calibrated against it fail together, and the document says only that the thresholds are unestablished there.

Consensus is reported as statement-level evidence and strength grades with no agreement percentages and no record of which proposed statements failed, so, as in the later Baveno conferences, the published document shows only what survived the room.

The extracted file is the accepted journal pre-proof: pagination and final figure placement are absent and inequality signs are unreliable in the extracted text, so the kilopascal and platelet thresholds that decide management must be checked against the published typesetting before use.
35120736.bottom_line: Establishes the definitions a liver surgeon now works to: clinically significant portal hypertension as an HVPG of 10 mmHg or more, ruled out by liver stiffness of 15 kPa or less with platelets of 150 x 10^9/L or more, ruled in at 25 kPa or more, with an ANTICIPATE-handled grey zone between, and it names clinically significant portal hypertension as a risk marker for decompensation and death after resection for HCC. It does not establish a threshold at which resection should be declined, and says so; the thresholds it does give are validated only in viral, alcohol-related and non-obese NASH disease, and in NASH cirrhosis the faculty concede portal hypertension can be clinically evident below the 10 mmHg definition. Use the numbers to describe risk, not to decide operability.

critique: This is a guidance, not a guideline, and the distinction carries the whole weight of its grading. There is no mandatory systematic review, no GRADE and no meta-analysis, and Strong Recommendations are permitted at Oxford Level 5, which is expert opinion. A reader who takes a Strong Recommendation here to mean what a strong GRADE recommendation means elsewhere is reading one word for two different things.

Panel disagreement is reported exactly once, on coffee, as '12 of 15 agree'. Every other statement is printed with no vote count, so the only place the panel is known to have been divided is visible because someone chose to print it, and the reader cannot tell whether the transplant, TACE or systemic-therapy statements were unanimous.

The strong recommendation for adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab after resection or ablation was made on an interim, recurrence-free-survival-only readout of IMbrave050 with no mature overall survival, and the guidance cites a Roche press release alongside the trial. The same authors withdrew the recommendation in 2025 when the benefit did not hold, which makes this statement a worked example of the grading problem rather than a position to act on.

Statement 44 advises against combining systemic with transarterial therapy for BCLC B outside a trial, reasoning that fewer than 20% of patients in the positive Asian trials were recruited outside the region and that TACE plus a tyrosine kinase inhibitor had failed in advanced disease. Phase 3 trials have since overtaken the position and the 2026 BCLC update incorporates them, so a reader using this document now is advised against a treatment that has become standard.

Radiotherapy is handled thinly. External beam radiotherapy and radiation segmentectomy appear only as alternatives to thermal ablation in BCLC A, with no stage-specific recommendation for stereotactic body radiotherapy or proton therapy, and the document adopts the BCLC 2022 algorithm as its Figure 9, carrying forward the same omission radiation oncologists had already objected to in print.

Transplant sections are built around US allocation policy: UNOS downstaging criteria, median MELD at transplant minus three exception scoring, OPTN class 5 imaging. These are administrative rules rather than biology and change on a different timetable from the evidence, so the recommendations date quickly and transfer poorly outside the United States, and the document does not say so.

Surveillance is set by incidence thresholds in Table 1 while the text concedes that no risk score is accurate enough to recommend. The thresholds are therefore applied through aetiology and fibrosis stage alone, which is the practice the risk scores were built to improve on, and the circularity is not acknowledged.

The table of expanded transplant criteria reports a single survival figure per criterion (UCSF 81%, total tumour volume under 115 cm3 75%, up-to-seven 71%, extended Toronto 68%, Kyoto 65%) with no confidence intervals and no indication that these come from different cohorts, eras and allocation systems. Set out as a list they invite the direct comparison the underlying studies cannot support.

The definitions that drive treatment are expert opinion presented as criteria. Table 5 lists factors making a patient TACE or Y-90 unsuitable and Table 6 defines refractoriness, but no threshold of tumour burden is given at which TACE becomes unsuitable, which is the decision those tables exist to serve; the 2026 BCLC update concedes the same gap.

Fifty numbered statements carry Oxford evidence levels, but the levels are not tabulated anywhere alongside the statements, so how much of the document rests on Level 5 can be established only by reading all fifty and counting.
