It does not establish its recommendations at the strength their labels imply: there was no mandatory systematic review, no GRADE and no meta-analysis, Strong Recommendations are permitted on expert opinion, and two of its positions, adjuvant immunotherapy and the prohibition on TACE plus systemic therapy, have since been reversed or overtaken. critique: Every recommendation reached consensus. The methods state that under EASL methodology there was no need to rewrite any recommendation because all found consensus, '100% did'. A Delphi in which nothing fails does not separate settled positions from contested ones, and the printed percentages bear this out: the lowest, 75% for bland transarterial embolisation as an alternative to conventional and drug-eluting bead TACE, is the floor of the band the document calls consensus.

The panel states that where trial data had not been fully reported, abstracts presented at international meetings were used as bibliographic references. Abstracts carry no protocol, no analysis plan and no peer review, yet they feed the same Oxford level-of-evidence scheme as full reports, and no recommendation is marked as resting on one.

No disclosures are printed. The conflict-of-interest section is a single pointer to ICMJE forms held elsewhere, so a reader weighing the panel's positions on SIRT, on checkpoint inhibitors or on drug-eluting beads cannot see who is paid by the manufacturers. Both the 2022 BCLC update and the 2023 AASLD guidance print theirs in full.

The AFP rule for transplantation conflicts with US practice and the guideline does not say so. EASL makes an AFP above 1,000 ng/ml an absolute contraindication whatever the tumour burden and requires 1,000 or less for three months before listing, whereas AASLD 2023 guidance and UNOS policy allow listing once an AFP of 1,000 or more falls below 500 ng/ml. The same biochemistry lists a patient in one jurisdiction and bars them in the other.

The prohibition on resection as a downstaging procedure is graded LoE 4 and drew 83% consensus, the lowest among the surgical items, yet is written as a prohibition. It rules out the resection-first with salvage-transplantation pathway used in several high-volume centres on the strength of expert opinion, without setting out the cohort data those centres have published.

SIRT is ruled out as an alternative to systemic therapy for portal vein invasion at LoE 3, strong, 86% consensus. The document's own narrative grounds this on SARAH and SIRveNIB, trials of intermediate and advanced disease in which dosimetry was not personalised, and does not engage DOSISPHERE-01, which randomised personalised dosimetry and reported better response and survival. The recommendation is stronger than the evidence the guideline itself lays out.

The ablation recommendation that no thermal technique is preferred over another, LoE 2 with strong consensus, is the correct reading of a failed superiority trial, and it appears in the same year that the BCLC group concluded microwave gives more reliable local control than radiofrequency up to 3 to 4 cm and should be preferred. Two European groups read the same two trials to opposite operational conclusions within twelve months and neither notes the disagreement.

Levels of evidence are assigned per recommendation without a table showing the number and design of studies behind each, so the reader must follow the narrative and its reference numbers. For the recommendations that decide a surgical case, resection for single HCC above 2 cm at LoE 2 and the minimally invasive approach where feasible, that narrative rests on observational series and propensity analyses whose selection bias the document acknowledges elsewhere but not there.

The guideline is explicitly partial and says so once, in a paragraph next to the corresponding-author footnote. There is no list of what is and is not covered, so a reader cannot tell which parts of a sixty-page document are current and which have been left to the 2018 guideline by silence.

In the extracted text the inequality signs are repeatedly mangled, so the thresholds that decide eligibility read as 'solitary HCC <-2 cm', '<-3 tumours' and '<-6.5 cm'. Every size and AFP cut-off in this copy must be checked against the published typesetting before it is used.

39693584.funding: Funded by Sun Yat-sen University's 5010 programme and the National Natural Science Foundation of China, with no declared conflicts of interest

A low quality-of-life completion rate precluded formal statistical analysis of that secondary endpoint

Transarterial radioembolisation was not permitted, so the control arm reflects chemoembolisation-dominant practice and the findings cannot be extended to radioembolisation
Race data could not be collected for 11 participants because participants in France cannot report race under local law

Nearly a third of participants were BCLC stage A and a further 10 percent stage C, so fewer than 60 percent had the intermediate-stage disease for which chemoembolisation is indicated, and the stage A patients were exposed to the full toxicity of a doublet systemic regimen

Grade 3 or worse treatment-related events occurred in 71 against 32 percent, immune-mediated events in 48 percent, and there were four treatment-related deaths including hepatic failure and immune-mediated hepatitis, in a population whose disease is confined to the liver and in whom curative options may remain

Chemoembolisation technique was prespecified by site and could be conventional or drug-eluting bead, with split procedures allowed and a maximum of two treatments per tumour, so the control intervention is heterogeneous across 137 sites and its quality cannot be audited from the report

Seventy-two percent of participants were Asian and 65 percent had hepatitis B, so the population does not match the metabolic and alcohol-related disease that dominates Western chemoembolisation practice
Patient-reported outcomes and quality of life are not reported, which is what would justify a progression-free survival endpoint at these rates of toxicity

The result is the first of four planned interim analyses, final for progression-free survival only, so the trial's own structure means the progression endpoint can no longer be tested while survival testing continues
The funders designed the study, collected and analysed the data, interpreted it and wrote the report, and the paper's own running header misprints the publication year

There is no arm receiving systemic therapy without chemoembolisation, so the question a tumour board faces for a patient with high tumour burden, whether to add chemoembolisation to systemic therapy rather than the reverse, is untouched
39798578.n: 480 of 847 screened patients with liver-confined unresectable HCC amenable to chemoembolisation, Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0 to 1, randomised 1:1 at 137 sites in 33 countries between May 2020 and January 2023 to lenvatinib plus pembrolizumab plus TACE (237) or dual placebo plus TACE (243); by BCLC stage 148 were A, 281 B and 50 C, and 72 percent were Asian
39798578.bottom_line: LEAP-012 is the first trial to show that adding lenvatinib and pembrolizumab to chemoembolisation prolongs progression-free survival in liver-confined HCC (median 14.6 against 10.0 months, HR 0.66). 39798578.funding: Funded by Merck Sharp and Dohme and Eisai, which had a declared role in study design, data collection, analysis, interpretation and writing of the report

limitations: Eligibility and TACE practice differ by region and randomisation was not stratified by site or country, which the authors state
Participants were not recruited from some high-incidence regions including Africa
Progression-free survival is a compound endpoint that might be confounded by competing deaths from cirrhosis in this population
Accessibility to the study and its regional variation might have been affected by socioeconomic or cultural factors
A full analysis of liver function is deferred until mature overall survival and subsequent-therapy data are available
critique: The primary comparison was changed by protocol amendment in August 2020, after the Independent Data Monitoring Committee had reviewed safety data and in response to the positive IMbrave150 result, from durvalumab plus placebo to durvalumab plus bevacizumab, so the hypothesis that the trial reports as primary was selected during the trial in the light of external evidence about which arm would win

The interim progression-free survival analysis did not reach significance and the result reported is the final analysis against a threshold of 0.044, so the trial became positive only at its second look

The interim overall survival analysis co-occurred with the reported final progression-free survival analysis, did not reach significance, and the data are withheld to maintain masking, so the only survival information in existence is negative and unpublished while the paper's Interpretation claims the potential to set a new standard of care

Durvalumab plus TACE was no better than TACE alone (HR 0.94), so the effect is attributable to bevacizumab, and without a bevacizumab-plus-TACE arm the contribution of the checkpoint inhibitor cannot be separated from that of the anti-VEGF antibody

The time-to-deterioration patient-reported endpoints using the EORTC QLQ-C30 and QLQ-HCC18 were key secondary endpoints and have not been formally tested under the multiple-testing procedure, so no quality-of-life result is available for a regimen that adds months of infusions to a locoregional treatment

Safety is reported by treatment received rather than as randomised, with denominators of 154, 232 and 200 against randomised arms of 204, 207 and 205, so the 39 patients assigned to the triplet who never received bevacizumab are counted in the doublet safety group; the resulting table shows no treatment-related deaths in the triplet against three in each of the other groups, which is an artefact of that accounting rather than a finding

Grade 3 to 4 oesophageal variceal haemorrhage occurred after bevacizumab dosing in 4 of 40 participants with baseline varices (10 percent) in the triplet and in none elsewhere, in a population whose portal hypertension is the reason they are having chemoembolisation

TACE modality, timing and number of procedures (one to four) were all left to the investigator, and bevacizumab was started only after the last TACE, so the trial tests a sequence rather than a defined regimen and its result cannot be mapped onto a specific protocol

The population spans BCLC A (about a quarter) to BCLC C (about a sixth) with half beyond up-to-7, chosen deliberately for breadth, so there is no stage for which the 15-month progression-free survival figure can be said to apply

PD-L1 status, one of the prespecified correlative endpoints, is missing in 23 to 25 percent of participants, and the association of PD-L1 and alpha-fetoprotein with progression-free survival is listed among the secondary endpoints without a result that would identify who benefits

A substantial list of prespecified secondary endpoints is explicitly not reported, including the direct comparison between the two durvalumab arms and progression-free survival after subsequent therapy, which are the analyses that would clarify the contribution of each component
Child-Pugh class B patients were randomised (2 to 3 percent per arm) despite the eligibility criteria, disclosed only in the baseline table

The funder had a role in design, collection, analysis, interpretation and writing, sponsor statisticians are among the authors and among those who accessed and verified the data, so no analysis independent of AstraZeneca underlies the result
39798579.n: 616 of 887 screened patients with unresectable HCC amenable to embolisation, BCLC A to C, randomised 1:1:1 at 157 sites in 18 countries between November 2018 and July 2021 to durvalumab plus bevacizumab plus TACE (204), durvalumab plus placebo plus TACE (207) or placebo plus TACE (205); about half were beyond up-to-7 criteria and 8 percent had portal vein macrovascular invasion
39798579.bottom_line: EMERALD-1 is the first positive phase 3 trial of systemic therapy added to chemoembolisation, with median progression-free survival improved by 6.8 months (HR 0.77). The primary comparison was switched by amendment during the trial to the bevacizumab-containing arm; durvalumab plus TACE alone gave a hazard ratio of 0.94, so the benefit appears to come from bevacizumab; the interim overall survival analysis did not reach significance and is withheld, and the patient-reported outcomes have not been tested.
39798579.funding: Funded by AstraZeneca, which had a role in study design, data collection, data analysis, data interpretation and writing of the report; sponsor statisticians are among the authors and most academic authors report AstraZeneca consultancy or honoraria

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that recurrence-free survival is a composite endpoint combining recurrence, which affects 40% of patients at three years, with death that may follow from cirrhosis or from treatment toxicity; that the initially positive and ultimately negative result may be explained by a lack of proportional hazards; that the episode is 'a cautionary note to assessing data at early interim time points' and underscores the importance of designing an interim analysis robust enough to call a trial positive under conventional stopping rules; that overall survival remained immature with more than 80% of patients alive in both arms at two years; that follow-up is continuing; and that non-proportional hazards in neoadjuvant and adjuvant HCC trials 'will require a thorough analysis' which they do not provide.
critique: The reversal and the recommendation it reverses carry the same label. Guidance statement 32 was a Strong Recommendation in 2023 and its negation is Level 1, Strong here, and both derive from interim analyses of one trial. The update offers no rule for when an interim readout is strong enough to recommend on, which is precisely the question its own cautionary note raises.

Reference 3, which supports the quoted account of the original positive result, is a Roche press release titled 'Roche's Tecentriq plus Avastin is the first treatment combination to reduce the risk of cancer returning in people with certain types of early-stage liver cancer in a Phase III trial', with no journal, year, date or locator. The update reproduces the 2023 guidance's citation of a company announcement instead of replacing it with the peer-reviewed report, in the document whose purpose is to correct what that announcement supported.

The updated analysis is cited only as Yopp et al., Annals of Oncology 2024;35:S1230, abstract LBA39. A Level 1 Strong recommendation against a whole class of perioperative therapy rests on a one-page conference abstract with no protocol, no analysis plan and no peer review.

The overall survival hazard ratio is 1.26 (95% CI 0.85 to 1.87), a point estimate favouring surveillance over treatment, and the authors print it and then write that recurrence-free and overall survival results were consistent across subgroups. A numerical signal of harm with an interval that excludes nothing clinically important draws no comment at all.

The recommendation extends beyond the evidence that prompted it. Statement 32 now advises against neoadjuvant as well as adjuvant systemic therapy at Level 1, Strong, but IMbrave050 was an adjuvant trial. The neoadjuvant evidence the update cites is a single-arm phase Ib study of 15 patients and a phase 2 study in which 20 patients underwent resection, so a Level 1 Strong recommendation against neoadjuvant therapy is issued without a randomised trial of neoadjuvant therapy.

The second interim analysis is still an interim analysis, at 35.1 months median follow-up with follow-up ongoing. The reversal therefore rests on data of the same kind as the data that produced the original error, and the update does not say what would make it change again or when it will be revisited.

Patients already receiving adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab under the 2023 recommendation are not mentioned. A guidance that created a treatment population withdraws the recommendation without saying whether those patients should stop, complete the eleven-to-twelve-month course, or be managed some other way.

Recurrence after adjuvant therapy is left to the revised Figure 11, which is the generic recurrence algorithm and draws no distinction for patients who have already had a checkpoint inhibitor. Prior exposure bears on salvage transplantation and on first-line systemic choice, and the 2023 document had at least addressed it by expert opinion.

The remedy offered for the methodological failure is a pointer rather than a method. The update cites a triple-negative breast cancer trial that used restricted mean survival time and says the hazards problem will require thorough analysis, but sets no endpoint standard, no alpha-spending requirement and no minimum follow-up for future HCC adjuvant trials, while naming four ongoing phase 3 adjuvant trials that will report under the same conventions.

The update says AASLD 'is considering innovative methods to bring timely updates, such as this one, to the field'. No process, trigger or interval is described, so the mechanism that produced this correction is not one a reader can rely on for the next one.

In the published version preserved text is in quotation marks and altered text is underlined. The underlining is lost in this extracted copy, so which sentences were changed and which were carried across cannot be determined from the text as read here.
39992051.bottom_line: Establishes that AASLD now advises against adjuvant and neoadjuvant systemic therapy after resection or local ablation for HCC, because the recurrence-free survival benefit of adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab in IMbrave050 did not hold at a second interim analysis (hazard ratio 0.90, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.12) while overall survival numerically favoured surveillance (1.26, 95% CI 0.85 to 1.87). It does not establish how to avoid the error it corrects: the reversal rests on a conference abstract and a still-interim analysis, carries the same Level 1 Strong label as the recommendation it overturns, extends to neoadjuvant therapy for which no randomised trial is cited, and leaves patients already on adjuvant treatment unaddressed. Its lasting value is as evidence about interim analyses rather than about atezolizumab.
39992051.funding: No funding statement appears anywhere in the three-page update. Two of the five authors declare conflicts: one consults for Exelixis, Genentech and AstraZeneca, and the senior author consults for Eisai, Merck, Roche, Genentech, AstraZeneca, Bayer, AbbVie, Sanofi, Moderna, Glycotest and Exelixis and sits on a data safety monitoring board for BMS, with all fees paid to his institution; the remaining three report none

limitations: Patients with Vp4 portal vein thrombosis were excluded

Open-label design; the authors state that although overall survival was not biased by the assigned treatment, the determination of adverse-event causality and health-related quality of life might have been influenced by awareness of treatment
The proportional hazards assumption was violated, so the authors report restricted mean survival time, piecewise hazard ratios and a MaxCombo test alongside the overall hazard ratio
The authors state that the cause of the early crossing of the survival curves is probably multifactorial
critique: The early excess of deaths is explained by the authors as an imbalance in deaths attributed to adverse events unrelated to study treatment, as assessed by investigators, so an excess of early deaths in the experimental arm of an open-label trial is set aside on the basis of unblinded causality judgments by the people delivering the treatment

The restricted mean survival time was similar between arms at 26 and 36 months and differs by only 2.8 months (95% CI 0.2 to 5.4) at 47 months, after nearly all follow-up had accrued, and the paper states that the restricted mean timepoints were explored post hoc

The cut-point for the piecewise hazard ratio was chosen by maximising the partial log likelihood over a grid of candidate timepoints, so the 6-month boundary that defines both the early hazard and the later benefit is data-derived rather than prespecified

Two protocol amendments between April 2019 and February 2023 changed the statistical assumptions to preserve power as events accrued, so the design against which the interim analysis was judged was revised during the trial

Tripling the response rate produced no progression-free survival advantage (9.1 against 9.2 months, HR 0.87, 0.72 to 1.06) and more progressive disease as best response, so the regimen's value for downstaging or for converting unresectable disease is unproven

No dose escalation or reduction was permitted for nivolumab or ipilimumab while dose reductions were allowed for lenvatinib and sorafenib, and treatment was capped at 2 years in the immunotherapy arm only, so the two arms were managed under different rules

All 332 treated immunotherapy patients had stopped treatment at cutoff but only 40 percent stopped for progression, against 69 percent of controls, so most discontinuations in the experimental arm were for toxicity or the protocol cap rather than for disease

Safety was an exploratory endpoint and no grade 5 treatment-related events are tabulated because grade 5 required death within 24 hours of onset; the 12 treatment-related deaths, 11 of them in the first 6 months, appear only in the text

The post hoc comparisons against each comparator separately give hazard ratios of 0.77 against lenvatinib and 0.42 against sorafenib, but only 50 patients received sorafenib, so the more favourable figure rests on a group smaller than most phase 2 trials
The control arm received later immunotherapy in only 13 percent of cases against 35 percent in the experimental arm, so post-progression care differed in the direction of the result

Eligibility excluded Vp4 invasion, significant ascites, grade 2 encephalopathy in the preceding year and prior transplantation, and required Child-Pugh 5 or 6, so the regimen's early hazard was measured in the fittest patients available

The comparator is a tyrosine kinase inhibitor at a time when immunotherapy combinations are first-line, so the trial cannot say whether this regimen should displace atezolizumab plus bevacizumab or durvalumab plus tremelimumab

The sponsor provided the agents, collaborated on design, collection, analysis and interpretation, employed or paid most authors and funded the writing of the first draft, and the four authors credited with the data analysis are sponsor-affiliated
40349714.n: 668 patients with unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh 5 or 6, ECOG 0 or 1 and no previous systemic therapy, randomised 1:1 at 163 centres in 25 countries between January 2020 and November 2021 to nivolumab plus ipilimumab (335) or investigator's choice of lenvatinib or sorafenib (333); of the 325 treated controls, 275 (85 percent) received lenvatinib and 50 (15 percent) sorafenib
40349714.bottom_line: CheckMate 9DW's preplanned interim analysis shows median overall survival of 23.7 against 20.6 months with nivolumab plus ipilimumab (HR 0.79, 95% CI 0.65 to 0.96, p = 0.018) and a tripled response rate, but the survival curves cross: mortality was 65 percent higher in the first 6 months (HR 1.65, 1.12 to 2.43) before separating in favour of the combination. 40349714.funding: Bristol Myers Squibb provided the trial agents and collaborated with the academic authors on design and on the collection, analysis and interpretation of the data, and funded medical writing including the first draft of the manuscript; four authors credited with the data analysis are sponsor-affiliated

limitations: About 90 percent of patients had a solitary tumour and more than half a largest diameter of 2 cm or less, so the authors state the result may best apply to a single tumour of 2 cm or less and that applying it to three nodules up to 3 cm would overestimate the findings

Patients whose tumour lay close to vasculature, the biliary tree or adjacent organs, or was poorly seen on ultrasound, were excluded if judged unfeasible for ablation, so the authors advise that ablation in difficult locations and above 2 cm needs careful indication
Because enrolment was discontinued, the analysis does not account for multiplicity across the two co-primary endpoints
Radiofrequency rather than microwave ablation was tested and open surgery was still common early in accrual, although the authors argue meta-analyses show no difference for either substitution
The number of patients who had a pretreatment biopsy is unclear, because biopsy was not routine in Japanese practice during the study period
LI-RADS criteria were not used; the authors state that by their own dynamic CT definition about 90 to 95 percent of the surgical patients were correctly diagnosed as HCC
In the observational cohort the groups were imbalanced at baseline, with a largest diameter of 2 cm or less in 50 percent of surgical against 72 percent of ablation patients
critique: The trial was designed to show the superiority of surgery and did not, with 67.2 percent power for a 10-point difference and 80 percent power only for 11.6 points, so this is a failed superiority trial; the Discussion nonetheless closes by asserting the equivalent effectiveness of both treatments

The local recurrence comparison was converted between reports: the same 12 and 24 events were 15.0 and 28.0 percent of patients with recurrence in 2022 (p = 0.07) and are 8.0 and 15.8 percent of all randomised patients here (p = 0.03), so a change of denominator turns a non-significant finding into the significant one the Discussion relies on

The definition of a successful ablation also changed: the 2022 report accepted RECICL TE4a or TE4b, explicitly including complete response without an adequate margin, while this report states success required TE4a with an adequate margin, so the two papers describe the same procedures by different standards

Several counts differ between the two reports of the same trial without explanation: 1,090 against 1,094 assessed, 778 against 782 declining randomisation, 7 against 6 patients excluded after registration, 151 against 152 eligible for ablation, and 25 against 35 patients lost to follow-up per arm

The paper reports Hochberg-adjusted p values of .84 for both co-primary endpoints while the limitations state that multiplicity was not accounted for; the adjustment simply assigns the recurrence endpoint the larger of the pair (unadjusted .50 becoming .84), and the paper contradicts itself about whether any adjustment was made

In the observational cohort the unadjusted recurrence-free survival favoured surgery (HR 0.80, p = .02) and after weighting became HR 0.84 with p = .08, so the headline of no difference rests on a p value crossing 0.05 rather than on the estimate changing, and the weighted curves in Figure 4 are footnoted as carrying unadjusted at-risk numbers

Recurrence was detected by MRI in 17.5 percent of surgical against 31.9 percent of ablation recurrences in the trial, so the arm with more local recurrence was also imaged more sensitively, and this asymmetry (p = .08) is tabulated without comment

Serious adverse effects were collected but post-treatment complications were not, giving 3.3 percent in the surgery arm and zero in 152 ablations, a figure the Discussion does not use but the abstract reports

Equal survival despite doubled local recurrence is achieved by an intensive salvage system: in the cohort, 26.3 percent of surgical recurrences were resected again against 5.2 percent of ablation recurrences, while 68.3 percent of ablation recurrences were re-ablated (p < .01), so the result describes Japanese retreatment capacity as much as the index procedure

The authors use the surgical arm's pathology to claim that 90 to 95 percent of patients were correctly diagnosed, which concedes that 5 to 10 percent of resected patients did not have HCC and leaves no corresponding check available for the ablation arm, where biopsy was rare

The SURF-Cohort consists of the 753 patients who refused randomisation and were treated by clinician preference, and is offered as a way to interpret and extrapolate the trial, when it embodies exactly the selection the trial was meant to remove: the paper's own forest plot shows surgery was chosen for tumours above 2 cm (OR 2.76) and ablation for low platelets and prior chemoembolisation
The Methods give 49 institutions and the Study Design 118, the same unreconciled discrepancy as in the 2022 report

Patients who died of other diseases without recurrence were censored rather than counted, in a cirrhotic population in which non-cancer death is a competing risk, and no competing-risk analysis of recurrence is presented
40554738.n: 1,094 patients assessed at 49 of 118 Japanese institutions between April 2009 and August 2015, yielding 302 in the randomised SURF-RCT (surgery 150, ablation 152) and 753 who declined randomisation in the parallel SURF-Cohort (surgery 382, ablation 371); 90 percent of the randomised patients had a solitary tumour with a median diameter of 1.8 cm
40554738.bottom_line: The final SURF report: 5-year overall survival was 74.6 percent after surgery and 70.4 percent after ablation (HR 0.96, adjusted p = 0.84) with recurrence-free survival 42.9 versus 42.7 percent (HR 0.90), and the 753-patient observational cohort agreed after weighting. Local recurrence was twice as common after ablation in both studies, the trial had 67.2 percent power for the 10-point difference it was designed to find, difficult tumour locations were excluded, and several figures including the local-recurrence denominators and the ablation success definition changed between this report and the 2022 one.
40554738.funding: Supported by the Japanese Foundation for Multidisciplinary Treatment of Cancer and Health and Labour Sciences Research Grant for Clinical Cancer Research H21-015; most authors report honoraria, research funding or advisory roles with industry, including Wako Diagnostics, Chugai, Eisai, AstraZeneca, Medtronic and Terumo

limitations: No limitations section; the authors concede only that no HVPG cut-off licenses resection in mild portal hypertension, that no AFP decline is defined as qualifying a downstaged patient for transplantation, that no strict cut-off separates TACE-eligible from TACE-unsuitable disease, that there is no consensus definition of major response and no staging framework for BCLC upon response, that the structural selection bias in the comparative observational literature 'cannot be fully eliminated', that overall survival is immature in the curative-intent trials and that some first-line radiotherapy trials failed to meet accrual targets, that evidence in portal vein invasion is limited with only 18 such patients in DOSISPHERE-01, and that the CUSE framework's effect on practice and outcomes has not been studied and its web tool is not yet developed.
critique: The methods are printed under the heading 'Data availability'. The PubMed search was restricted to humans, adults over 19 and English-language records, which removes much of the Japanese and Chinese literature on particle therapy, hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy and conversion surgery; Japanese proton therapy investigators wrote to the journal to say particle therapy is not integrated into the strategy, and the language restriction is part of why.

Two of the three evidence syntheses underpinning the update are the authors' own: an individual-participant-data meta-analysis of external beam radiotherapy in about 5,000 patients and an aggregate-data meta-analysis of 73 studies in macrovascular invasion. The group that sets the algorithm also produced the evidence that moved it, and the update does not treat that as a source of bias.

CUSE is a process presented as an advance. It names four dimensions, prescribes GO, CONSIDER and NO-GO thresholds and points to a web tool at bclccuse.ai, and the authors concede the tool is not developed and the framework's effect on practice and outcomes has not been studied. A tumour board gains a vocabulary and no reproducible rule, and CUSE is also where the structural selection bias in the observational literature is said to be 'explicitly acknowledged' rather than addressed.

EBRT and TARE enter the figure for BCLC 0 and A on data the update itself qualifies in the same paragraphs: RASER with a mean tumour size of 2.1 cm and standard deviation 0.4, LEGACY with a median of 2.6 cm and a range to 8.1 cm, and an EBRT literature described as limited by heterogeneity and selection bias with trials that failed to meet accrual. The position changed; the class of evidence did not.

Microwave is made the preferred percutaneous technique up to 3 to 4 cm. The randomised comparison on which that rests failed to show superiority of microwave over radiofrequency, and EASL, reading the same trials in the same period, recommends no preference. The update neither notes the disagreement nor explains what turns a null trial into a preference.

The update refuses to present cross-trial hazard ratios or survival-curve metrics so as not to imply a hierarchy unsupported by direct evidence, then admits four first-line doublets to BCLC C with no means of choosing between them. The refusal is methodologically defensible and leaves the clinician holding the decision the document exists to inform.

BCLC D survival is revised from about three months to under twelve without the data behind the revision being set out. A prognostic estimate that moves fourfold between editions of the same algorithm, having been used in the interim to decide against active treatment, needs an account of why it changed.

The divergence from the 2023 AASLD guidance on adjuvant systemic therapy is stated without engaging the 2025 AASLD critical update, which reversed that guidance and now agrees with BCLC. The reader is left to discover elsewhere that the disagreement has resolved.

Figure 4 argues that progression-free survival is an unreliable surrogate for overall survival because the same interval can be produced by indolent progression, lethal progression, aggressive biology or treatment-related death. The argument is correct, and the update does not apply it to its own reliance on objective response, complete pathological response and local control in the BCLC 0 and A recommendations it has just expanded.

Complete pathological response is used as supporting evidence across modalities with incompatible denominators: 34% versus 20% on explant in a UNOS retrospective comparison of TARE and TACE, 25% in a series of 88 patients given SBRT, and 'frequent' after superselective TACE, while the same passage notes that radiologic complete response does not consistently predict histologic necrosis. The figures are set side by side and are not comparable.

The competing-interest record is corrupted in this copy: one author's entry ends 'and grants from;' with no list, another repeats the same company list twice, and a third reads ': ; none'. For a document whose recommendations now favour named devices and agents, the disclosures as published here cannot be read in full.
41151697.bottom_line: Establishes the current BCLC algorithm, bringing external beam radiotherapy and radioembolisation into early-stage disease, preferring microwave to radiofrequency up to 3 to 4 cm, admitting ECOG 2 and four first-line doublets to BCLC C, defining multifocal disease numerically and revising BCLC D survival upward from three months to under twelve. It does not establish the thresholds that decide individual cases: no HVPG cut-off for resection with portal hypertension, no AFP decline for downstaging eligibility, no cut-off for TACE-unsuitable disease, no definition of major response, and a decision framework whose effect on practice the authors say has not been studied. The positions moved, and most of them moved on observational and single-arm evidence the update itself qualifies.
41151697.funding: No commercial funding for the update; grant support is listed author by author from Instituto de Salud Carlos III, CIBER and CIBEREHD, AECC, World Cancer Research, an EASL registry grant and institutional research support, with several authors reporting none. The authors note that BCLC A patients have a favourable prognosis and that the medicalisation required by these regimens may have conferred undue risk without commensurate benefit
Neither trial addressed whether adding locoregional therapy to systemic therapy improves outcomes, only the reverse
Chemoembolisation modality, technique and selectivity were variably reported in both trials
Delayed initiation of bevacizumab in EMERALD-1 may have blunted its effect
Progression-free survival is not a validated surrogate for overall survival in this setting

critique: The review is an expert narrative with no systematic search, no inclusion criteria and no evidence grading, so its appraisal cannot be separated from the judgment of its four authors

All four authors declare consultancy or advisory relationships with the manufacturers of both regimens under review, so the only published independent-sounding appraisal of these trials is written by people paid by their sponsors

The review disclaims cross-trial comparison and then tabulates the two trials side by side, although they differ in eligibility (Child-Pugh B7 and Vp1 to Vp2 invasion allowed in one and excluded in the other), in chemoembolisation schedule and in the sequencing of the systemic agents, so the table invites the comparison the text forbids

The RECIST version 1.1 response figures are internally inconsistent across the paper: Table 1 gives 44 against 30 percent and 47 against 37 percent, the body text gives 41.0, 43.6 and 29.8 percent and 47 against 33 percent, and Figure 2 gives 43.6 against 29.6 and 46.8 against 33.3 percent, so a reader cannot establish from the review what either trial's response rate was
Figure 2's own panel misprints the progression-free survival confidence interval as 12.6 to 10.0 and the hazard ratio confidence interval as 0.15 to 0.84, neither of which is a possible interval

The review states that quality-of-life data are needed to justify a progression-free survival endpoint at these toxicity rates and then reaches a practice conclusion without them, so its own standard of evidence is not met by its own recommendation
The alternative it raises, giving the same drugs sequentially after progression rather than concurrently, is never tested against any data, and no trial addressing it is identified

The review takes the regulatory approval of both regimens as the context for its scepticism but offers no analysis of the regulatory reasoning, so the reader is left with a disagreement between the authors and the agencies rather than an argument that settles it
No formal assessment of either trial's risk of bias is attempted, in a review whose central claim is that the trials' endpoints are insufficient
41503570.bottom_line: A narrative review by two interventional radiologists, a hepatologist and a medical oncologist arguing that the progression-free survival gains in LEAP-012 and EMERALD-1 do not yet justify routine adoption of chemoembolisation plus immunotherapy without survival or quality-of-life data. Its most useful observation is that over 40 percent of each trial lay outside intermediate stage and that neither trial had a systemic-therapy-only arm, so the question of whether to add chemoembolisation to systemic therapy remains unasked.
41503570.funding: No funding statement is identified for the review; all four authors declare consultancy or advisory relationships with the sponsors of the regimens reviewed, including AstraZeneca, Merck, Eisai, Genentech and Boston Scientific

limitations: Open-label design and lack of statistical power for subgroups, carried over from the primary report
The post hoc up-to-7 subgroup analysis was not prespecified and can only be considered hypothesis-generating

The relative risk of recurrence changed over time, so the Cox hazard ratio is an aggregation of time-varying hazards and should be interpreted with caution; the authors suggest restricted mean survival time would be more accurate
The authors state that the imbalance in deaths together with the reduced recurrence-free survival benefit shifts the benefit-risk assessment negative, particularly after curative-intent treatment
The authors state that the updated results do not support use of the regimen in the adjuvant setting and that the effect on late recurrences of different aetiology is unclear
critique: The surveillance arm's median recurrence-free survival (36.0 months) is longer than the treated arm's (33.2 months) and recurrence occurred in 49 percent of each arm, so the stratified hazard ratio of 0.90 is the aggregate of a curve that crosses rather than a residual benefit

The authors' own leading explanation for the transient effect is that bevacizumab may impair radiological detection of relapse while it is being given, which, if true, means the primary endpoint of the trial was measurably biased by the drug and the original positive interim result was an artefact of surveillance imaging rather than only an unsustained benefit

The curves separated at 3 months, reached maximum difference at 9 months and intersected at about 2 years, and the hazard-rate analysis places the peak of recurrence at 6 months in the control arm against 18 months in the treated arm, so twelve months of treatment moved recurrence by roughly the duration of treatment

The post hoc up-to-7 analysis that is offered as a path forward has a hazard ratio above 1 in the within-up-to-7 group, so the proposal to treat only high-burden patients rests on a subgroup split whose other half suggests harm

Ninety-nine surveillance patients (30 percent) crossed over, some after a second resection or ablation, and one surveillance patient was mistakenly treated and counted in the treated safety population, so neither survival arm is a clean comparison

Death was the commonest reason for leaving the study and was more frequent in the treated arm (54 of 334, 16 percent, against 46, 14 percent), and the overall survival hazard ratio of 1.26 is reported as immature rather than as a signal requiring explanation

Immune-mediated adverse events occurred in 208 of 332 treated patients (63 percent) against 59 of 330 (18 percent), with 9 percent needing systemic corticosteroids, all in patients who had been rendered disease-free

Of 914 patients assessed, 57 already had residual, recurrent or metastatic disease and 26 had no signed consent form, so the eligibility screen for an adjuvant trial let through questions about whether all enrolled patients were truly disease-free at randomisation

The analysis is descriptive by design because the interim was declared positive, so the trial that changed guidance can no longer be tested on the endpoint that changed it, and the authors recommend for future trials the longer follow-up and non-proportional-hazards methods their own design lacked
Restricted mean survival time is proposed in the limitations as the more accurate measure of effect but no restricted mean survival time estimate is reported anywhere in this paper

Five authors are Roche or Genentech employees holding company stock, the sponsor funded the medical writing, and the figure that frames the paper is reprinted and adapted from the sponsor's own earlier positive report
41580093.n: The same 668 randomised IMbrave050 patients reanalysed at a 3 May 2024 cutoff with a median follow-up of 35.1 months and a minimum of 29.2 months; 99 of 334 surveillance patients (30 percent) had crossed over to atezolizumab plus bevacizumab
41580093.bottom_line: The descriptive final analysis of IMbrave050 shows the interim recurrence-free survival benefit was not sustained: median recurrence-free survival 33.2 months with treatment against 36.0 months with surveillance, stratified HR 0.90 (95% CI 0.72 to 1.12), recurrence in 162 of 334 against 164 of 334, and overall survival numerically worse (HR 1.26, 0.85 to 1.87). One year of adjuvant atezolizumab plus bevacizumab deferred early recurrence without preventing it, at the cost of 63 percent immune-mediated events and an excess of deaths.
41580093.funding: Sponsored by F. Hoffmann-La Roche, which provided the drugs and collaborated on design, collection, analysis and interpretation; five authors are Genentech or Roche employees holding Roche stock and medical writing was sponsor-funded

limitations: Retrospective design with non-random treatment assignment, which the authors state
Institutional heterogeneity in protocols and supportive care
BCLC misclassification between investigator-reported and adjudicated stage, since staging was re-adjudicated from component variables because reported staging was discordant and often missing

Formal violation of the proportional hazards assumption for several covariates in all four models, so the authors say their hazard ratios should be interpreted with caution and report 3-year restricted mean survival time instead
Confounding of the proton versus photon comparison by geography, access and insurance, which the authors acknowledge
The authors concede that advanced-stage patients included were those most suitable for radiotherapy, with liver-dominant disease
critique: The conclusion that radiotherapy survival is comparable with resection, thermal ablation and other ablative locoregional therapies rests on a comparison with guideline expectations rather than on any measured difference, because the dataset contains no resection, ablation or chemoembolisation arm

Only 30 of 96 eligible centres (31 percent) contributed, and the centres were identified because they had already published favourable technical standards and outcomes, so centre-level selection and publication selection both push the survival estimates upward

The internal pattern of the results shows how severe the selection is: treatment-naive BCLC B patients survived 6.3 years, longer than the whole BCLC B group and longer than treatment-naive BCLC A patients, which is not a possible ordering for a stage-based prognostic system and indicates that the stage labels no longer carry their usual meaning in this cohort

Re-adjudicating every patient with an ECOG score above 0 into BCLC C may have moved merely comorbid or cirrhotic patients out of the early-stage groups and so inflated early-stage survival, which the authors note but do not quantify
The apparent proton advantage was not a prespecified hypothesis, so the covariates that would be needed to interpret it, tumour volume, dose, fractionation and dosimetric goals, were never collected
Treatment spans 2000 to 2024, pooling planning, immobilisation, image guidance and motion management technologies that differ by a generation, with year of treatment entered only as a covariate
Sixty percent of patients had prior locoregional therapy, so for most of the cohort radiotherapy was salvage after another treatment rather than the first-line option the paper's framing invites

Table 4 in the published text contains corrupted confidence intervals (a hazard ratio of 0.82 with an interval of 0.72 to 0.03 and one of 1.60 with an interval of 1.41 to 1.28), and Table 2's modality proportions disagree with the narrative, so the paper's own numbers cannot all be read as printed

The journal's own relevance note frames radiotherapy as a treatment to be considered and further investigated in trials rather than as established first-line therapy, which is a materially weaker claim than the paper's conclusion
42139645.n: 4,913 patients treated with ablative liver external beam radiotherapy at 30 of 96 invited centres in 11 countries, pooled as individual patient data after a systematic review to 15 December 2022; 60 percent had received prior locoregional therapy and there was no comparator arm
42139645.bottom_line: The largest individual-patient dataset on ablative liver radiotherapy, reporting median overall survival by adjudicated BCLC stage and concluding that outcomes are comparable with resection and ablation. There is no comparator of any kind, only 31 percent of eligible centres contributed and they were identified by having published favourable results, 60 percent of patients had prior locoregional therapy, and the proportional hazards assumption was violated in all four Cox models.
42139645.funding: Coordinated by the University of North Carolina for the EBRT Collaboration Group and registered as PROSPERO CRD42023467399; no industry funding is identified

limitations: No limitations section; the faculty concede only that recommendations from earlier conferences not specifically revised here remain valid, including the whole of HVPG measurement methodology, that the criteria for diagnosing clinically significant portal hypertension carry 'individual limitations' which statement 1.16 asks the clinician to consider without naming them, that non-invasive tests for clinically significant portal hypertension and high-risk varices may not be applicable where there is macrovascular invasion (1.21, LoE 3, weak), that patients in the indeterminate range are handled by re-evaluation at 12 months on LoE 4 weak evidence, and that 153 topics remain open on the research agenda, among them the incidence of and value of six-monthly surveillance for HCC in Budd-Chiari syndrome and whether Milan and AFP-based listing criteria apply in that setting.
critique: The reference list contains seven items, all of them previous Baveno conference reports published between 1992 and 2022. Two hundred and seventy-two statements carry a graded level of evidence, the three new HCC statements among them at LoE 3, with no citation to a single primary study, so no grade in this document can be traced to the evidence that produced it.

No disclosures are printed for any of the 84 faculty while the acknowledgements thank fifteen industry partners for financial support. Echosens manufactures the vibration-controlled transient elastography platform to which the footnote on statement 1.15 ties every liver stiffness threshold in the document, and Mindray makes ultrasound systems; a conference part-funded by the makers of the measuring devices has issued the cut-offs at which those devices decide management, and names no competing interest.

Baveno VII's participants declared they had nothing to disclose regarding funding or conflict of interest while acknowledging unrestricted grants. Baveno VIII drops the declaration altogether rather than extending it to the industry support it now names, so disclosure in this series has moved from implausible to absent.

Only statements reaching the threshold are published, and the document says so. Nothing shows how many statements were voted on, which failed, or how the agreement figures were distributed, so a reader cannot separate a settled position from a contested one that was dropped; the printed agreement figures run from 80% to 100% and those at the bottom of that range are indistinguishable from statements that never appeared.

Strong consensus is defined as above 80% faculty agreement. Four in five is a low bar for a document that presents itself as consensus, and it means a statement opposed by up to one voting expert in five is printed without that dissent being visible anywhere.

The three HCC statements are all new, LoE 3 and weak, yet written as operational rules. Statement 1.22 extends the rule-out of clinically significant portal hypertension across BCLC stages 0 to C and licenses omitting endoscopy; 1.23 restricts the ANTICIPATE route to BCLC 0 to A 'without large (>5cm) nodules in the right liver lobe'. The 5 cm figure and the right-lobe restriction are stated with no derivation, so the reader cannot tell whether they come from data, from an argument about hepatic vein compression, or from the discussion in the room.

Statement 1.21 withdraws the non-invasive tests exactly where an HCC board needs them, saying they may not be applicable when there is macrovascular invasion, and offers no alternative. The patient in whom portal pressure matters most is returned to unguided judgement, and the retained Baveno VII statement linking clinically significant portal hypertension to decompensation and mortality after resection for HCC still names no threshold at which resection should be declined.

The statements that bear on surgery are not new work. The link between clinically significant portal hypertension and post-resection outcome, and the whole of HVPG methodology, sit in the summary box of prior statements that 'remain valid' but were not re-examined. The box then asks the reader to interpret those statements 'in the context of current Baveno VIII recommendations which favor non-invasive tests over routine HVPG measurements', which is to apply the conclusions of an invasive reference standard through tests this conference has not validated against it in this population.

Thresholds are specific to device, frequency and measurement conditions, spleen stiffness above 55 kPa at 100 Hz and liver stiffness by vibration-controlled transient elastography, but no guidance is given for centres using other elastography platforms or point shear-wave techniques. The aetiology caveat that matters most appears as a parenthesis in the figure, 'except in obese MASLD', rather than being carried into the statements themselves.

This is an accepted journal pre-proof dated 31 July 2026: the statements may change at copy-editing, pagination is absent, and no independent editorial or commentary on Baveno VIII was indexed in PubMed when this record was made, so the document has had no published external scrutiny.

The paediatric statements are new and were voted by the same faculty, with paediatric hepatologists added to only some panels and the composition of the vote for each statement not reported. The paediatric symposium held alongside the conference was sponsored by a single children's hospital, and the research agenda concedes that paediatric cut-offs for varices still need validation.
42624290.bottom_line: Establishes the current consensus thresholds for ruling clinically significant portal hypertension in and out without catheterisation, extends them for the first time to patients with HCC across BCLC stages 0 to C, and tells a tumour board that endoscopy may be omitted when liver stiffness is 15 kPa or less with platelets of 150 x 10^9/L or more. It does not establish any of this as validated practice: the three HCC statements are new, LoE 3 and weak, the 5 cm right-lobe caveat is unexplained, the tests are withdrawn where there is macrovascular invasion, and the whole document carries seven references, all to earlier Baveno meetings, so no statement can be checked against the evidence behind it. Take the numbers as the field's working agreement, not as a tested rule.
42624290.funding: The acknowledgements record financial support from fifteen named industry partners, among them Echosens, Mindray, Boehringer Ingelheim, Roche/89bio, Madrigal, Grifols, GSK, Cook, CSL and W.L. Gore, alongside scientific partner organisations including EASL, ESGE, AEEH, AISF, BASL, CIBEREHD, JSH and VALDIG; no conflict-of-interest or disclosure statement for any of the 84 faculty members appears anywhere in the document

limitations: Over-representation of participants from Asia, which the authors concede
Open-label design, although the study was sponsor-blinded with centralised randomisation and blinded central review of the primary endpoint

Heterogeneity in treatment practices and investigator-driven post-randomisation decisions around progression, including repeat chemoembolisation and subsequent anticancer therapy, which the authors say could influence outcomes
Findings concern chemoembolisation only, so combinations with transarterial radioembolisation remain unstudied
The cause of a small number of deaths could not be established and remained classified as unknown
The authors note frequent lenvatinib dose modification and discontinuation for adverse events as a reflection of the tolerability burden
critique: The allocation ratio was changed from 1:1:1 to 1:1 during the trial after external trials were reviewed, so the doublet arm consists of the first 175 patients enrolled and is compared with a non-concurrent portion of the control arm; because the triplet's survival comparison failed, the doublet's results were never formally tested at all

Overall survival did not improve and the restricted mean survival difference of 1.48 months has a confidence interval spanning zero, so the trial's clinical value rests entirely on a progression endpoint at 40 percent survival maturity

Post-discontinuation systemic therapy was given to 29 percent of the triplet arm against 53 percent of the chemoembolisation arm, so the control group received more subsequent treatment, which works against the survival result the trial failed to show rather than explaining it away
Adding lenvatinib worsened toxicity without improving response over the doublet, so the component the trial made its primary comparison is the one that adds harm without adding efficacy

Grade 3 to 4 treatment-related events occurred in 63 against 19 percent, serious adverse events in 64 against 23 percent, and there were seven treatment-related deaths including two from myocarditis, in a population still eligible for embolisation
PD-L1 status is missing in about 80 percent of participants, so the only candidate biomarker is unavailable in four patients out of five

Repeat chemoembolisation and post-progression therapy were at investigator discretion in an open-label trial, and 55 percent of procedures were conventional against 42 percent drug-eluting bead, so neither the control intervention nor the post-progression pathway is standardised

The abstract quotes maximum grade 3 to 4 adverse events of any cause (hypertension 34 of 287, 12 percent) while Table 3 gives treatment-related grade 3 to 4 hypertension as 29 of 287 (10 percent), so the toxicity figures in the summary and the table are not the same quantity

Two separate data cutoffs are reported in one paper, progression-free survival on 2 September 2025 and overall survival on 23 February 2026, with a third cutoff still to come, so the efficacy and survival results describe different datasets
The online version required correction on 28 September 2026, so the figures as first published were not reliable
There is no arm receiving the systemic regimen without chemoembolisation, so the incremental value of the embolisation itself in a patient who could have systemic therapy alone is not addressed
AstraZeneca funded the trial, several authors are its employees, and sponsor staff are among those who accessed and verified the data
42636832.n: 760 of 1,124 screened patients with Child-Pugh A HCC not amenable to resection, ablation or transplantation but amenable to chemoembolisation, randomised at 177 sites in 21 countries between March 2022 and November 2024 to tremelimumab-durvalumab (STRIDE) plus lenvatinib plus TACE (293), STRIDE plus TACE (175) or TACE alone (292); 61 percent were beyond up-to-7, 10 percent had Vp1 or Vp2 invasion and 72 percent were Asian
42636832.bottom_line: EMERALD-3 shows that dual checkpoint blockade plus lenvatinib added to chemoembolisation prolongs progression-free survival, but overall survival did not improve (HR 0.84, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.09, p = 0.18) at 40 percent maturity with a restricted mean survival difference of 1.48 months (-1.21 to 4.16). The allocation ratio changed mid-trial so the doublet arm is a non-concurrent subset of 175 patients that was never formally tested, and grade 3 to 4 treatment-related events were 63 against 19 percent with seven treatment-related deaths.
42636832.funding: Funded by AstraZeneca; several authors are AstraZeneca employees and sponsor staff are among those who accessed and verified the data

limitations: With only four recurrences the analyses of T stage, nodule number, alpha-fetoprotein and capsule had very low power, which the authors state explicitly in the Results
27 percent of tumours were assigned too low a stage before surgery despite angiography and CT arterial portography, so preoperative staging did not identify the group that did well
The study does not address transplantation versus resection for a small resectable HCC: unresectability was a requirement for entering the trial, as the authors state

Pre-transplant chemoembolisation was not randomly assigned but given only when liver function was not seriously impaired, so the comparison of treated and untreated patients is confounded, as the authors concede

Recurrence-free survival rises above overall survival after three years because recurrence was excluded at autopsy in some patients who died and because data were censored earlier, an artefact the authors note
The authors state the results need confirmation by others and that transplantation should be offered only for unresectable tumours until randomised data exist
critique: Survival is counted from transplantation, not from listing: of 60 patients listed, 1 died waiting and 11 were still waiting at the census date, and none of the 12 appear in any survival analysis, so the figures describe the patients who got a graft rather than the patients selected by the criteria

The 85 percent versus 50 percent comparison is a comparison of correctly staged against understaged patients, not a test of the criteria: the limits were set before enrolment but assessed only on the explanted liver, so the division is made after the organ has been used and cannot be reproduced prospectively

The four-year estimates rest on almost no one at risk: Figure 1 shows 5 patients at risk at 48 months and Figure 3 shows 3 criteria-met and 3 criteria-not-met patients at risk at that point, with no confidence interval given on either survival difference

The whole prognostic separation is driven by four recurrence events in 48 patients, three of them in the understaged group; no multivariable model is fitted and no adjustment is made for the fact that the understaged group also had larger and more numerous tumours

Only 2 of the 8 deaths were from recurrent cancer; the rest were perioperative bleeding, sepsis, pulmonary embolism, recurrent HBV, post-transplant lymphoproliferative disease and chronic rejection with aspergillosis, so overall survival in this cohort measures transplant mortality more than tumour biology

The three patients who died within one month were counted as recurrence-free on the stated assumption that they had not lived long enough to recur, which moves early deaths into the favourable column of the recurrence-free endpoint

Diagnosis of HCC was accepted on an alpha-fetoprotein above 300 ng/mL without biopsy in some patients, and 15 patients had a single lesion of 2 cm or less, so the cohort may include nodules that were not HCC while the explant series reports a median tumour diameter of only 1.5 cm

Explant pathology, which defines the within-criteria group, was read after 26 of 48 patients had received one to four cycles of lipiodol chemoembolisation; treatment that shrinks or devitalises nodules will move patients into the favourable group, and no sensitivity analysis excluding the pretreated patients is offered

Vascular invasion and nodal metastasis were found in none of the 48 explants, which is implausible for a series with up to 11 nodules per liver and suggests the pathological protocol (1 cm slices, hilar nodes only) was not sensitive to microvascular invasion, the very feature used to justify the limits

Every comparator in the Discussion is historical and drawn from the literature: 25 percent three-year survival for untreated small HCC, 70 percent four-year survival in the European Liver Transplant Registry for cirrhosis alone, and 0 to 56 percent five-year survival after resection; there is no contemporaneous control group of any kind

One of the four recurrences was a subcutaneous implant along the track of the pre-transplant diagnostic liver biopsy, so a quarter of the recurrence events were iatrogenic consequences of the staging algorithm the paper relies on, and this is reported without comment on the risk of seeding

The acknowledgements thank staff of Sandoz, Fujisawa and Knoll, and the Discussion advances a claim about corticosteroid-sparing immunosuppression and recurrence risk, while the article carries no conflict-of-interest disclosure
8594428.n: 48 patients with cirrhosis and unresectable early-stage HCC transplanted between January 1991 and December 1994, drawn from 60 listed and 295 patients with HCC seen at one Milan centre; 35 of the 48 were confirmed within the tumour limits on explant pathology
8594428.bottom_line: Establishes that transplantation can give 75 percent four-year survival and 83 percent recurrence-free survival in cirrhotic patients with a single HCC of 5 cm or less or up to three nodules of 3 cm or less, and that tumours exceeding those limits do much worse. It does not validate the limits as a selection rule, because they were applied to explant pathology in the same 48 patients that generated them, with only four recurrences, no external cohort, and no analysis from the point of listing.
8594428.funding: Supported by the Italian Association for Cancer Research; no conflict-of-interest statement appears anywhere in the article, and the acknowledgements thank staff of Sandoz, Fujisawa and Knoll

limitations: Unresolved decompensation was intentionally screened for, which the authors say probably explains their 38 percent rate against the lower figures in retrospective series
Hepatic vein catheterisation is not performed routinely in most centres, as the authors concede, and the non-invasive alternatives they examined were significant only on univariate analysis
The authors cannot explain why a lower blood urea nitrogen was associated with decompensation and note that the values stayed within the normal range
The authors note that mean bilirubin was within the normal range in both groups, so a normal bilirubin does not rule out the risk of postoperative decompensation

The authors state that their recommendation rests on patients selected by the best available criteria at one centre in one era, and defend the result against alternative explanations by reference to their own concurrent surgical series
critique: Forty-four clinical, laboratory, tumour and haemodynamic parameters were screened univariably and six carried into a logistic regression fitted to 11 events, so the model is overfitted by any standard and the odds ratio of 1.90 per mmHg (95% CI 1.12 to 3.22) is not a stable estimate

The dichotomy is perfectly separating (11 of 15 versus 0 of 14), and a logistic regression containing a near-perfectly separating covariate does not produce trustworthy coefficients or p values; the reported P = 0.0001 for the multivariable term is no stronger than the univariable comparison it repeats

No derivation of the 10 mmHg threshold is described: no cut-point search, no receiver-operating analysis and no alternative thresholds are reported, because 10 mmHg is the conventional definition of clinically significant portal hypertension carried over from the variceal literature and applied here after the fact

The cohort mean gradient was 9.9 plus or minus 4.4 mmHg, so the cut-point sits almost exactly at the mean of a narrow continuous distribution, which is the split that maximises apparent separation and the one least likely to reproduce

The endpoint is not liver failure: 16 of the 17 early events were ascites, all 11 unresolved events had ascites requiring diuretics with one jaundice and one encephalopathy, and the single death was septic shock with multiorgan failure, so the guideline-shaping outcome is diuretic-requiring ascites at 3 months

Ascites management was protocolised (40 mEq sodium, furosemide and spironolactone as needed) by the same unblinded team that had measured the gradient, so the endpoint of requiring diuretics is partly a treatment decision by clinicians who knew the exposure

The paper reports no survival outcome of any kind, yet its recommendation is that resection be restricted; recurrence was in fact numerically more common in the group without decompensation (9 versus 4), and the claim that decompensation shortens survival is supported only by the authors' own prior abstract

No postoperative haemodynamic measurement was made in any patient, so the mechanism offered, unchanged portal inflow through a reduced non-compliant vascular bed, is imported from a rat model and never tested in this cohort

The authors conclude that surgical factors cannot explain the findings because resection type, ischaemia time and transfusion did not differ, but those comparisons are made between 11 and 18 patients and have essentially no power to exclude a surgical effect

Two of the six univariable predictors point in directions the authors cannot account for, a lower blood urea nitrogen and a bilirubin difference within the normal range, which is what fitting six variables to 11 events in 29 patients produces

The gradient was measured once, in the right hepatic vein, within 10 days of surgery, with no repeat measurement, no reproducibility estimate and no interobserver data, in a study where the clinical decision turns on a few mmHg either side of the cut-point

Follow-up for the endpoint stops at 3 months and no longer-term liver or oncological outcome is reported, so the paper cannot show that the patients it would exclude from resection do better with any alternative

The Discussion's proposed algorithm ends by recommending percutaneous ethanol injection as potentially radical only in tumours larger than 3 cm, the opposite of the finding in the reference it cites for that claim, which reported that efficacy falls with increasing tumour size
No conflict-of-interest statement appears, and the same group went on to embed this single-centre threshold in the BCLC staging system and in the EASL and AASLD recommendations it now underwrites
8831597.n: 29 consecutive Child-Pugh A cirrhotic patients with HCC (28 of 29 solitary and under 5 cm) resected at one Barcelona hospital between May 1991 and June 1994; 11 developed unresolved hepatic decompensation at 3 months
8831597.bottom_line: The index study behind the rule that resection should be restricted to patients without portal hypertension: in 29 Child-Pugh A patients, 11 of 15 with a hepatic venous pressure gradient of 10 mmHg or more had unresolved decompensation at 3 months against none of 14 below that gradient. The separation is perfect in a cohort of 29 with 11 events screened against 44 candidate variables, the 10 mmHg line was imported rather than derived here, the endpoint is almost entirely diuretic-requiring ascites, and no survival outcome is reported at all.
8831597.funding: Supported in part by grants from the Fondo de Investigaciones Sanitarias (FIS 93/0544 and 94/0757) and the Direccion General de Investigacion Cientifica y Tecnica (DGICYT PB94-1562); no conflict-of-interest statement appears in the article
